claims.text: AI-generated code volume outruns fixed human review capacity, making code review the bottleneck on shipping software
claims.note: One large telemetry study reports code output rising far faster than shipped software after agent adoption, but attributing the gap to review is the authors' inference and other bottlenecks (testing, deployment, product decisions) are not separated out.

claims.text: Reviewer defect-finding effectiveness drops sharply once a single review exceeds a few hundred lines
claims.note: The SmartBear Cisco field study found defect density per line falling past roughly 200-400 lines per review, though it is a single vendor-run industrial dataset rather than a controlled experiment.

claims.text: A change passing its test suite is a weak proxy for whether a maintainer would actually merge it
claims.note: Tests only cover specified behaviour and cannot see maintainability, scope or hidden coupling; the METR maintainer study cited here supports this, though it is one study on agent-written PRs.

claims.text: Running several independent automated review passes and keeping only agreed findings reduces false positives and improves review quality
claims.note: Ensemble and self-consistency effects are well documented for language models, but the size of the review-quality gain rests on one academic paper and vendor reports.

claims.text: Automated code reviewers are fooled by confidently framed malicious changes far more often than human reviewers
claims.note: Prompt injection against LLM reviewers is a documented weakness and vendors warn about it themselves, but the specific human-versus-agent comparison comes from a single study.

claims.text: Teams that stop reading agent-written code accumulate hidden defects that later force large rewrites
claims.note: Supported by a public retraction and by audits of agent-ported code finding unusual numbers of unsafe constructs, but the evidence is anecdotal with no controlled comparison.

claims.text: Assigning people to review code full time to absorb more volume burns reviewers out
claims.note: Review fatigue and the tedium of full-time review are widely reported by practitioners, but there is no measured burnout study specific to this arrangement.

claims.text: The human role in code review is shifting from reading diffs to designing and tuning the systems that inspect code
claims.note: A forecast about how roles will evolve rather than a claim that can be checked against evidence.

claims.text: Writing tests after the code leaves holes in the suite because hard-to-test code gets skipped
claims.note: The mechanism is plausible and matches practitioner experience, but controlled TDD studies measure defects and productivity rather than coverage gaps, so the size of the effect is not established.

claims.text: Writing tests first forces the code to be decoupled and testable by construction
claims.note: Studies of TDD find modest improvements in some internal quality metrics such as coupling and cohesion, with mixed results overall and effects that depend on developer experience.

claims.text: A test suite with known gaps gives no decision value when it passes, so it cannot be trusted
claims.note: A framing about what trust in a suite means rather than a measurable outcome; partial suites still catch some regressions.

claims.text: Test-first development reduces time spent debugging
claims.note: Controlled studies show TDD lowers defect density at some cost in development time; direct measurements of debugging time are scarce.

claims.text: Making a failing test pass gives a small reward that makes test-first more enjoyable than writing tests afterwards
claims.note: A claim about enjoyment and motivation that varies by person.

claims.text: A trustworthy automated test suite lets developers change and deploy code without fear
claims.note: Survey research such as DORA links reliable test automation with higher delivery confidence and performance, but the direction of causation is not isolated.

claims.text: Having the whole team at one keyboard eliminates waiting for answers to blocking questions
claims.note: The mechanism follows directly from having all needed skills present, and mob case studies report it, but there is no controlled comparison and it depends on the product owner being present too.

claims.text: Mob programming finishes stories in hours that took individuals working separately weeks
claims.note: Self-reported from one team with the speaker himself saying the card comparison is not proof; no independent measurement of mob throughput exists.

claims.text: Working as one group on one stream of work removes merge conflicts
claims.note: A single group working on one branch has nothing to merge, so this follows by construction and is consistently reported by mob teams.

claims.text: Mob programming onboards new members quickly and spreads knowledge so the team does not depend on one person
claims.note: Case studies and surveys of mob teams consistently report faster knowledge spread, but no study measures onboarding time against a control.

claims.text: Switching tasks to fill time while blocked creates work-in-progress inventory instead of fixing the queueing problem
claims.note: Lean and queueing theory plus context-switching research support the cost of multitasking and partially done work; the inventory framing is a model rather than a measurement.

claims.text: Sustained mob programming requires members to treat each other with kindness, consideration and respect
claims.note: A team norm whose necessity cannot be separated from the practice in available evidence.

claims.text: Pairing or mobbing puts the best of each participant into the code and rarely the worst
claims.note: Pair programming meta-analyses show modest quality gains at higher effort, with effects depending on task complexity and pair expertise; no measurement exists for mobs.

claims.text: Short daily retrospectives keep improvement on track better than infrequent longer ones
claims.note: Plausible by analogy to frequent feedback loops but no study compares retrospective cadence.

claims.text: Static typing catches type errors at compile time before code reaches users
claims.note: Journal version of the same experiment: the compiler points to the exact location of a type error, whereas the dynamic system finds it at run time with symptoms that may appear far from the cause, which is why Groovy subjects needed more navigation and more test runs.

claims.text: Static typing yields better runtime performance because the compiler knows each variable's memory layout
claims.note: Conflates typing with ahead-of-time compilation; static languages are usually faster, but JIT compilers make dynamic languages competitive and types are only one of several causes.

claims.text: Dynamic typing is faster for prototyping and rapid iteration
claims.note: Scripts (Perl, Python, Rexx, Tcl) took a median 3.1 hours versus 10.0 hours for C, C++ and Java and were half as long, but the author attributes this to built-in associative arrays and the absence of declarations, times were self-reported for the script group, and the result is explicitly limited to the phonecode problem.

claims.text: Static typing suits safety- and performance-critical domains while dynamic typing suits fast-iteration domains
claims.note: A description of adoption patterns and taste rather than a measurable benefit claim.

claims.text: Most software developers, including game developers, work roughly normal hours with only occasional overtime
claims.note: Industry surveys such as IGDA's find crunch still common in games with roughly half of respondents reporting it, so the picture is mixed; the video's own survey is small and self-selected.

claims.text: Crunch is a symptom of poor planning, especially failing to schedule testing and iteration time
claims.note: Postmortems and case studies link crunch to scope and schedule failures, but publisher deadlines, funding and studio culture also drive it, so planning is one cause among several.

claims.text: Sustained crunch lowers productivity and employee happiness
claims.note: Labour economics and reviews of overtime research show output per hour falls and errors rise after sustained weeks beyond roughly fifty hours, and burnout studies link crunch to attrition.

claims.text: Much developer overtime is self-imposed from passion rather than mandated by employers
claims.note: Surveys find both self-driven and management-driven crunch, and normative pressure makes voluntary overtime hard to separate from expected overtime.

claims.text: Long-horizon task estimates are inaccurate and managers should not rely on them
claims.note: Review of time-prediction studies finds average error of 20-30% and no general bias, but software projects of at least 100 work hours show a median overrun of about 20%, so large-scope estimates are biased low rather than useless.

claims.text: Smaller companies tend to have somewhat more overtime than larger ones
claims.note: Based on a small informal survey; broader data on company size and hours in software is inconsistent.

claims.text: Game features need more iteration than business software because feel and fun cannot be specified on paper
claims.note: A judgment about the nature of the work rather than a measurable claim.

claims.text: Long-lived branches delay integration and produce merge conflicts that grow with team size
claims.note: The mechanism is direct, and DORA research associates short-lived branches and trunk-based development with higher delivery performance.

claims.text: Running a CI server is not continuous integration if branches live for days or weeks
claims.note: Matches the standard definition of continuous integration as frequent integration to a shared mainline, which tooling alone does not guarantee.

claims.text: Trunk-based development with one small change per release increases release frequency and makes rollbacks easier
claims.note: DORA data correlate trunk-based development with better delivery metrics and small changes are easier to revert, but the gains are correlational and the team's own numbers are self-reported.

claims.text: Feature flags let unfinished work merge to trunk and decouple deployment from release
claims.note: A well-established mechanism used at scale by large web companies, with documented costs in flag management.

claims.text: Reusing an old feature flag can switch on dormant code paths with catastrophic results
claims.note: The Knight Capital incident is documented in the SEC order as a repurposed flag plus an incomplete deployment, and flag hygiene guidance exists because of such cases.

claims.text: Trunk-based development only works with a fast comprehensive test suite and same-day code review
claims.note: Practitioner accounts and DORA both treat fast automated tests as a prerequisite for continuous delivery; synchronous review is one way to meet the merge cadence but not the only one.

claims.text: Ephemeral per-branch environments remove the bottleneck of shared test environments
claims.note: The queueing mechanism is sound and widely reported, but evidence is practitioner case studies and the environments bring their own cost and data-seeding work.

claims.text: Trunk-based development is unsuited to products that must tightly control released versions
claims.note: Release branches cut from trunk are a standard way to ship versioned products from trunk, so the limit is weaker than stated, though strict version control does reduce the practice's advantages.

claims.text: Developers who deploy their own work to production are happier because they see its impact
claims.note: DORA surveys associate continuous delivery with lower burnout and higher job satisfaction, but causation is not isolated and this is one team's impression.

claims.text: Feature flags carry an ongoing removal cost that teams must schedule and pay back
claims.note: Stale-flag debt is well documented and large companies have built tooling specifically to remove dead flags.

claims.text: Writing a test per method and mocking every dependency couples tests to implementation so refactoring breaks them
claims.note: Over-specified interaction tests are a documented cause of fragile suites in both practitioner literature and studies of test co-evolution.

claims.text: Writing tests slows delivery by a meaningful fraction compared with not writing them
claims.note: Controlled studies of TDD report roughly fifteen to thirty-five percent more initial development time alongside fewer defects, so the slowdown is real but is partly repaid later.

claims.text: In TDD the unit of isolation is the test, not the class under test
claims.note: A definitional reading of Kent Beck's book rather than an empirical claim.

claims.text: Customer-readable acceptance test suites are rarely read by customers and carry a heavy maintenance burden
claims.note: Practitioner consensus including the Fit author's own retraction supports this, though some teams report value from Gherkin-style specs; no controlled study exists.

claims.text: Getting a test to green with quick dirty code and then refactoring is faster than engineering the design up front
claims.note: Kent Beck's original claim, consistent with cognitive-load arguments against solving and designing at once, but not directly measured.

claims.text: The refactoring step needs no new tests because behaviour is unchanged and already covered
claims.note: Practice advice that follows from the definition of refactoring; whether existing tests actually cover the behaviour is case by case.

claims.text: Tests written to probe implementation details should be deleted once they have served their purpose
claims.note: A judgment about test maintenance trade-offs with no empirical comparison.

claims.text: Slow UI-driven end-to-end test suites are fragile and break on cosmetic changes
claims.note: Flaky and brittle UI tests are extensively documented in industry reports and flaky-test research, which is why the test pyramid pushes coverage downward.

claims.text: Moving to open-plan offices reduces face-to-face interaction and shifts communication to email and messaging
claims.note: Two Fortune 500 headquarters moved from cubicles to open floors; wearable badges and server logs showed face-to-face time fell 72% (5.8 to 1.7 h per person per day) at the first firm and 67-71% at the second, while emails sent rose 56%, received 20-50% and IM messages 67%; quasi-experiment without a control group, 52 and 100 participants.

claims.text: Open-plan offices increase noise and visual distraction that impairs focused work
claims.note: Large occupant surveys such as Kim and de Dear find open-plan workers less satisfied, especially on noise and privacy, with no offsetting gain in ease of interaction.

claims.text: Alternating collaboration with individual work produces better solutions than either constant collaboration or isolation
claims.note: The Bernstein, Shore and Lazer intermittent-collaboration experiment found this pattern, though on abstract problem-solving tasks rather than software work.

claims.text: Taking on small third-party dependencies for trivial functions adds fragility out of proportion to the code saved
claims.note: The left-pad incident and subsequent supply-chain research show deep transitive dependency trees in npm expose projects to removals and malicious updates.

claims.text: Coding conventions spread by repetition rather than understanding, producing cargo-cult practices
claims.note: A sociological framing about how practices propagate.

claims.text: Comments that restate code are noise and drift out of date because nothing checks them
claims.note: Studies find comment-code inconsistency common after change, but comprehension research also shows explanatory comments help readers, so the claim holds for restating comments not all comments.

claims.text: Work expands to fill the time and headcount given to it
claims.note: Parkinson's law and Brooks's law have anecdotal and some experimental support for deadline effects, but the ten-versus-hundred example is a single anecdote.

claims.text: Applying design patterns such as factories everywhere makes code harder to understand than direct code
claims.note: Prechelt's controlled pattern experiments found patterns help only when their flexibility is needed and otherwise add comprehension cost.

claims.text: Names carry most of a program's design intent, so vague names like Manager signal weak design
claims.note: Identifier studies show descriptive names improve comprehension; the specific heuristic about vague suffixes is expert opinion.

claims.text: Logging without stated requirements grows until it dominates the codebase
claims.note: Anecdotal from client codebases; no measurement of logging proportion across projects.

claims.text: A single-process monolith is the right default and microservices need a specific justifying outcome
claims.note: A footnote states it is important to avoid premature decomposition of new systems into services, which can inhibit delivery performance, citing Fowler's MonolithFirst; this is an authorial assertion, not a measured result.

claims.text: The main benefits of microservices are independent deployability, data isolation and organisational autonomy
claims.note: Practitioner surveys and case studies report these as the realised motivations, alongside maintainability and operational costs that offset them.

claims.text: Microservices cost more in the short term and rarely save money
claims.note: Operational overhead of distributed systems is well documented and several public cases of consolidating back to a monolith cite cost; evidence is case studies not controlled data.

claims.text: Deploying one small service limits the scope and risk of each release compared with redeploying a whole monolith
claims.note: Smaller change sets do carry less risk, but as Fowler notes in the same conversation the distributed system adds integration risk a monolith can test end to end, so the net effect depends.

claims.text: Coordination cost grows faster than linearly with team count on a shared codebase, which service boundaries contain
claims.note: Communication-path growth is the classic Brooks argument and Conway-style case studies support boundaries helping, but there is no controlled measurement of microservices reducing coordination.

claims.text: Process boundaries enforce modularity that in-process modules fail to because languages let developers violate them
claims.note: Architecture erosion studies confirm in-process modules decay, but distributed monoliths show process boundaries get violated too via shared databases and chatty coupling.

claims.text: Splitting a shared relational database is the hardest part of decomposition and gives up joins and transactions
claims.note: Loss of cross-service joins and ACID transactions is intrinsic to the approach and migration literature consistently names data as the main difficulty.

claims.text: Adopting microservices without changing the organisation yields the costs without the benefits
claims.note: Consistent with Conway's law research and practitioner reports, but it is an expert judgment rather than a measured outcome.

claims.text: Services that always change together should be merged or re-sliced
claims.note: A design heuristic; co-change analysis can detect the pattern but whether merging is right is a judgment.

claims.text: Static typing produces fewer bugs and more readable code in large systems
claims.note: Large GitHub studies found a small defect advantage for static typing that weakened on replication, and bug-detectability studies suggest a type checker catches a minority of real bugs, so the benefit is real but modest.

claims.text: Type inference gives static typing with dynamic-like brevity, removing most of the old verbosity trade-off
claims.note: Inference clearly cuts annotation burden in Go, Rust and TypeScript, but compile times, generics complexity and type-error comprehension remain costs.

claims.text: DORA metrics measure delivery velocity and stability but do not translate directly into business outcomes
claims.note: DORA's own reports find the four keys correlate with organisational performance, so a link exists, but it is indirect and does not say whether features were the right ones.

claims.text: DORA metrics are retrospective and cannot be acted on until after code has shipped
claims.note: They are lagging indicators by construction, though teams routinely act on their trends, so the practical limitation is smaller than framed.

claims.text: Pull requests spend about half their lifetime idle waiting for someone
claims.note: A vendor dataset with a product to sell, though independent studies at Google and Microsoft also find review wait time dominates review cycle time.

claims.text: Small pull requests are picked up and merged faster
claims.note: Regression on about 40,000 merged, CI-tested pull requests from 40 GitHub projects finds that pull requests adding more lines and more commits take significantly longer from creation to close, with size and discussion length the dominant predictors; an observational preliminary study of open-source projects.

claims.text: Smaller changes mean less rework, fewer incidents and faster restoration
claims.note: DORA's small-batch findings and defect-per-line research support the direction, but the evidence is correlational and vendor-sourced.

claims.text: Developers do not care about DORA metrics, only about merging their code quickly
claims.note: A generalisation about motivation that varies by team.

claims.text: Automatically approving trivial changes and routing risky ones to senior reviewers speeds flow without losing safety
claims.note: Risk-based review routing is plausible and used at large companies, but the benefit here rests on a vendor's product claim with no independent measurement.

claims.text: Line coverage shows code was executed, not that the tests check its behaviour
claims.note: Across 31,000 generated suites on five large Java systems, coverage correlated only low-to-moderately with mutation-detection effectiveness once suite size was controlled, so high coverage does not indicate an effective suite; executing a line does not reveal an error in it.

claims.text: Mutation score measures test suite quality better than coverage does
claims.note: Just et al. found mutant detection correlates with real-fault detection, with caveats about mutant representativeness.

claims.text: A surviving mutant reveals either a missing test or code that can be removed
claims.note: A surviving mutant may be an equivalent mutant (e.g. == changed to >= with identical behaviour) rather than a missing test, and manual inspection is needed to tell; the study classified up to 35% of mutants as equivalent, so the either/or omits a third case.

claims.text: Mutation testing is too slow to run routinely without parallelisation or incremental selection
claims.note: Runtime is the documented adoption barrier; Google's deployment runs mutation analysis only on changed lines for this reason.

claims.text: Equivalent mutants cannot be detected automatically and require human judgment
claims.note: Manual inspection is required because automatically determining whether a mutant is equivalent is undecidable, which is why studies fall back on assuming anything the master suite misses is equivalent.

claims.text: Higher-level behavioural tests make mutation testing more practical than many fine-grained unit tests
claims.note: A practitioner hunch; fewer larger tests may run slower per mutant, so the net effect on runtime is unclear.

claims.text: Full line coverage is relatively easy to reach when a team is motivated
claims.note: Achievable for many codebases but costly for legacy or hardware-bound code; coverage-driven tests are often weak, which is the speaker's own point.

claims.text: An AI reviewer can take an automated first pass at a pull request before a human reviews it.
claims.note: AI review tools do produce first-pass comments; how much of the human review they replace is not independently measured.

claims.text: Summarizing a change and its risks helps a reviewer understand unfamiliar code faster.
claims.note: Change summaries plausibly cut orientation time, but there is little independent measurement of review speed or defect-finding with AI summaries.

claims.text: Keeping review feedback, discussion and fixes in one tool removes the context switching that slows review.
claims.note: Context switching has measurable cost in general, but the size of the gain from tool consolidation is a vendor claim without independent data.

claims.text: Software delivery speed and stability move together rather than trading off; the best teams get both.
claims.note: Six years of survey data show speed and stability are outcomes that enable each other: cluster analysis finds elite performers do significantly better on all four metrics and low performers worse on all, rather than trading throughput for stability.

claims.text: Industry and regulatory status do not predict whether DevOps practices improve delivery performance.
claims.note: Controlling for industry, DORA found no evidence that industry affects SDO performance except retail (which did slightly better), including highly regulated financial services and government; organisation size over 5,000 employees did predict lower performance.

claims.text: Emergency changes made under stress usually skip testing, which is when testing is most needed.
claims.note: Skipped testing in emergency changes is widely reported in incident reviews but not quantified here.

claims.text: High-performing teams rely on automated test suites and reserve manual effort for exploratory testing.
claims.note: DORA reports less manual testing among elite performers, but this is a self-reported association rather than a measured cause.

claims.text: Infrequent releases leave security patches and compliance updates waiting months to reach production.
claims.note: Patch latency follows directly from lead time; the risk exposure is real though its magnitude varies.

claims.text: Shipping code that has not been exercised by a unit test is unprofessional, and TDD is the surest way to avoid it.
claims.note: Authors concede that following the test-first rule prevents shortcuts that skip tests, but an ethnographic study found developers wrote more production code than needed, omitted refactoring and let tests fall behind even when nominally test-first; the 'unprofessional' judgment is not testable.

claims.text: Driving architecture from unit tests without an up-front domain model yields a procedural, bottom-up design that cannot be refactored out of.
claims.note: Design damage from test-driven isolation is reported in case studies and the DHH debate, but controlled studies of TDD's design effects are mixed and small.

claims.text: Architecture should evolve incrementally, informed by executing code and tests, rather than be designed in full up front.
claims.note: Incremental architecture is standard agile practice, but there is no controlled evidence it beats moderate up-front design and both debaters endorse some up-front structure.

claims.text: Some domain structure must be fixed up front because incremental refactoring cannot reach the right architecture from a naive starting point.
claims.note: Large-scale architectural decisions are known to be costly to reverse, but how much up-front design is needed is unresolved.

claims.text: Design by contract covers the whole input range of a method, giving broader assurance than sampled unit tests.
claims.note: Contracts specify behaviour over all inputs but are only enforced on executed inputs unless statically verified, so coverage gains depend on tooling.

claims.text: Class-level unit tests are hard to trace to business value.
claims.note: A judgment about traceability rather than a measurable claim.

claims.text: The 10x spread between fastest and slowest programmers is mostly noise: a programmer's own task-to-task variation is as large as the variation between programmers.
claims.note: Re-analysis of 61 experiments (614 subjects) finds the slowest-quarter to fastest-quarter median ratio is typically 2-3x and max/min ratios above 10 are rare, so the 10x spread is an artifact of best-vs-worst comparison; the report does not measure a programmer's own task-to-task variation.

claims.text: Experience, lines of code written and degrees held did not predict programmer productivity.
claims.note: This null result holds in the PSP dataset, but other studies find modest effects of relevant experience, so it is not settled.

claims.text: Productivity differences across programmers follow a long-tailed log-normal distribution, not a bell curve.
claims.note: Work time distributions across 1491 observations show a clear long right tail (skewness about 1 to 2) and a normal assumption over-estimates variability almost always; the paper confirms long-tailed non-normal shape but does not fit a log-normal.

claims.text: Small tasks are easier to estimate and reveal runaway work early enough for the team to intervene.
claims.note: Estimation error grows with task size in most estimation research; the early-intervention benefit is plausible but less directly measured.

claims.text: Shortening sprints too far increases estimation uncertainty because each sprint samples less work.
claims.note: Statistically sound for sprint-level forecasting, but no study pins down where the diminishing returns begin.

claims.text: Hiring super-programmers is a poor route to team productivity compared with improving the working environment.
claims.note: Follows from the variance finding, but environmental interventions have not been compared head-to-head with hiring in controlled studies.

claims.text: TDD biases design toward extra abstraction and indirection, which harms clarity unless the designer pushes back.
claims.note: Test-induced indirection is widely reported in practice and in the DHH debate, but controlled studies of TDD on design quality show small mixed effects.

claims.text: Unit tests alone cannot catch integration errors, so a suite of only unit tests does not make code self-testing.
claims.note: By construction isolated unit tests do not exercise component interaction; integration failures are a well-documented defect class.

claims.text: The right mix of unit and higher-level tests depends on where a system's complexity lives, not on fixed pyramid ratios.
claims.note: Reasonable and consistent with practice, but no study compares test-mix strategies against outcomes.

claims.text: Higher-level tests often pay back better than unit tests at finding bugs in integration-heavy code.
claims.note: Integration and system tests do catch defects unit tests miss, but relative cost-effectiveness depends on the system and is not well quantified.

claims.text: Estimates become deadlines, and deadlines drive the overtime that destroys sustainable pace.
claims.note: Deadline pressure is a documented driver of overtime, but the chain from estimate to crunch is not inevitable.

claims.text: Hitting an estimate has no value if the software built is the wrong thing.
claims.note: A framing about what counts as success rather than a measurable claim.

claims.text: Story points get converted back into time, defeating their purpose of keeping estimation away from the clock.
claims.note: Widely reported in practice surveys, but there is no measurement of how often it happens.

claims.text: Team velocity is mostly set by organizational obstacles, so teams cannot raise it by working harder.
claims.note: Organizational friction does affect throughput, but velocity also varies with skill and task mix, so 'only' is too strong.

claims.text: Simply counting completed stories forecasts delivery as accurately as story-point estimation.
claims.note: Vasco Duarte's project data and some team analyses show story count tracks points closely, but this depends on stories being similarly sized.

claims.text: Most of a long backlog is wasted because items far down will change before they are reached.
claims.note: Requirements volatility is well documented; the claim that distant items are nearly worthless is plausible but unmeasured.

claims.text: Short fixed-budget increments let the business decide early whether to continue or kill a project, reducing risk without estimates.
claims.note: Incremental funding does reduce exposure, but cancelling early still needs some forecast of what remains.

claims.text: Organizations with high software delivery performance are more likely to meet their commercial and non-commercial goals.
claims.note: DORA's SEM finds SDO performance predicts organisational performance on commercial and non-commercial goals, and elite performers are twice as likely to meet or exceed their organisational performance goals; both sides are self-reported in a cross-sectional survey.

claims.text: Maturity models go out of date too quickly to guide technology transformations.
claims.note: An argument about how to frame a transformation, not a measured outcome.

claims.text: Technology alone does not raise performance; it must be combined with lean management and organizational culture.
claims.note: DORA's models and Bessen's HBR work support IT-plus-management, but the specific synergy is modeled, not experimentally shown.

claims.text: A loosely coupled architecture that lets teams test, deploy and change independently predicts delivery performance more than the platform or technology used.
claims.note: DORA 2017 found architecture the strongest predictor of continuous delivery while mainframe and greenfield status were not significant; still survey-based.

claims.text: Lightweight change approval within the team outperforms heavyweight external change approval boards.
claims.note: Respondents whose organisations require CAB or senior-manager approval were 2.6 times more likely to be low performers, formal approval showed no association with lower change failure rates, and a clear, lightweight change process made teams 1.8 times more likely to be elite.

claims.text: A generative, high-trust, blameless organizational culture predicts software delivery and organizational performance.
claims.note: Westrum culture measures predict performance in DORA's structural models, with survey-based data.

claims.text: Transformational leadership is necessary but not sufficient for high delivery performance.
claims.note: DORA found the bottom third of leaders half as likely to be high performers while top leaders were no better than median; one survey year.

claims.text: High-performing delivery teams report less deployment pain and burnout and are more likely to recommend their workplace.
claims.note: Self-reported associations in DORA data; direction of causation is not established.

claims.text: Fatigue raises the rate of catastrophic errors, so an overworked team can make net negative progress.
claims.note: Fatigue-error links are well documented; net negative team progress is a plausible extreme rather than a measured average.

claims.text: Long working hours raise rates of injury, illness, cardiovascular disease and mental health problems through chronic stress.
claims.note: Large epidemiological studies link long hours to injury, stroke and depression; stress biomarkers provide a mechanism.

claims.text: Crunch does not improve product outcomes; it correlates with slightly worse ones.
claims.note: The Gamasutra/IGDA survey analysis found this; it is a single self-reported dataset but no study shows crunch improving outcomes.

claims.text: Sleep deprivation impairs cognition like alcohol intoxication and blinds people to their own impairment.
claims.note: Dawson and Reid's equivalence studies and later work show sleep loss impairs performance like alcohol and degrades self-assessment.

claims.text: Caffeine tolerance builds within days, so it cannot offset extended overtime.
claims.note: Tolerance to caffeine's alerting effects develops within days to a week in most studies, though partial benefits persist for some.

claims.text: Letting workers choose their own hours improves satisfaction, health and productivity.
claims.note: Schedule control shows consistent positive associations in occupational health research, but effects are moderate and mostly observational.

claims.text: A full day of rest after a missed night of sleep does not restore performance to baseline.
claims.note: Shift-work recovery studies support incomplete recovery after one night; the size depends on the deficit.

claims.text: Rewriting a working system from scratch throws away accumulated bug fixes and hands years of lead to competitors.
claims.note: Netscape, Borland and similar cases support it, but successful rewrites exist, so the harm depends on scale and context.

claims.text: Code is harder to read than to write, so programmers misjudge old code as a mess.
claims.note: Comprehension consumes most maintenance effort in studies, supporting the premise; the inference about misjudging old code is plausible but untested.

claims.text: Architectural problems can be fixed by incremental refactoring without discarding the codebase.
claims.note: Incremental re-architecture is widely practiced and documented, but some structural changes are impractical without large rewrites.

claims.text: A rewrite team is unlikely to do better because it lacks the original team's experience and repeats old mistakes.
claims.note: Second-system effects are documented, but a rewrite with clearer requirements can succeed.

claims.text: Performance problems concentrate in a small part of a system, so targeted optimization beats a full rewrite.
claims.note: Hotspot concentration is a well-established profiling finding; the exact ratio varies.

claims.text: Dynamic languages became popular because they gave fast feedback and concise syntax for early web work, not because dynamic typing is inherently better.
claims.note: A plausible historical account consistent with language-adoption timelines, but causal attribution from history is not testable.

claims.text: In-editor type errors give faster feedback than running the program and tracing a crash.
claims.note: All indicators (time, test runs, files opened, file switches) favoured the static type system on type-error tasks because the compiler names the location while a run-time failure appears far from the cause; the feedback came from a compiler in a plain text editor, not an in-editor checker, so the claim's in-editor form is an extrapolation.

claims.text: Gradual typing requires a more complex type system and keeps dynamic runtime overhead, so it is not the best of both worlds.
claims.note: Type-system complexity in TypeScript and Sorbet supports this, though gradual typing's migration benefit is real.

claims.text: Non-blocking type errors keep the fast feedback of static types without preventing you from running code or tests.
claims.note: TypeScript's emit-on-error demonstrates feasibility; the productivity claim is anecdotal.

claims.text: Nearly every mainstream language that emerged after the 2000s is statically typed.
claims.note: Consistent with RedMonk and similar rankings, with a few exceptions.

claims.text: Pull-request review delays feedback and pushes developers to batch changes, making daily integration impossible.
claims.note: Review latency is a measured delay in PR studies, but many teams integrate daily with small PRs, so the incompatibility is not absolute.

claims.text: Asynchronous review loses the two-way conversation that makes review educational and lets the author explain intent.
claims.note: Synchronous review has documented knowledge-sharing benefits, but asynchronous tools also support discussion; the loss is a matter of degree.

claims.text: Pull requests were designed to gatekeep untrusted open-source contributors and fit poorly inside a trusted team.
claims.note: Inside a single trusted company, all 44 surveyed Google engineers agree code review is valuable and gatekeeping/security oversight are among its stated purposes, which argues against review fitting poorly in a trusted team; the claim's history of pull requests is not addressed.

claims.text: Pair programming provides continuous code review without adding a separate review step that slows delivery.
claims.note: Pairing does catch defects as they are written, but pairs cost more person-hours, so 'without slowing' depends on the measure.

claims.text: Most developers who try pair programming end up preferring it.
claims.note: Williams' student studies found high post-trial preference, but professional adoption surveys show persistent dislike among many.

claims.text: Pairs sustain focus better than individuals working alone.
claims.note: Reported in pair-programming studies as 'pair pressure', mostly self-reported.

claims.text: Every comment is a failure to express intent in code and should be treated as a necessary evil.
claims.note: Comments had only 33% relative predictive power for readability judgments, less than blank lines; the authors suggest comments appear where code was already less readable so the two balance out, giving neither strong support for comments nor for treating them as failures.

claims.text: Editors render comments in muted colors, which trains developers to ignore and neglect them.
claims.note: Syntax highlighting conventions do de-emphasize comments; whether that causes neglect is untested.

claims.text: Complex generic type annotations slow development in statically typed languages on simple algorithmic tasks.
claims.note: Found in this 21-student study for Java generics; generalization beyond Java-style generics is uncertain.

claims.text: Controlled experiments show statically typed languages have usability advantages over dynamically typed ones.
claims.note: The paper's own literature review says existing evidence is partially contradictory, with some studies favouring dynamic, some static and some inconclusive; its experiment adds evidence for static typing on class-identification and type-error tasks but none on semantic-error tasks.

claims.text: Static typing forces implementing an entire interface up front even when only part of it is used.
claims.note: True of Java-style nominal interfaces; languages with structural typing or default methods avoid much of this cost.

claims.text: Most software projects run late or over budget, with few finishing early.
claims.note: Systematic review found no general overoptimism in software when small tasks are included, but projects of 100+ hours had a median overrun of about 20%, i.e. more than half of larger projects overran while small tasks were unbiased or overpessimistic.

claims.text: The paper that introduced the waterfall diagram warned that the approach was risky and invited failure.
claims.note: Royce's 1970 paper does say the simple sequential model is risky and invites failure and recommends iteration.

claims.text: Replacing guesswork with measured experiments is what makes software development an engineering discipline.
claims.note: A philosophy of practice rather than a measurable claim.

claims.text: Continuous delivery yields order-of-magnitude improvements in quality and efficiency, not incremental gains.
claims.note: DORA shows large gaps on deployment metrics between clusters, but order-of-magnitude gains in cost or quality rest on a few case studies.

claims.text: Short cycle times force small teams, automation and fewer handoffs, so continuous delivery drives out lean and agile practices as a side effect.
claims.note: Logically coherent and consistent with DORA's capability model, but the causal direction is asserted, not measured.

claims.text: Automating everything except creative judgment makes releases repeatable and reliable because humans are not.
claims.note: Deployment automation correlates with lower change failure in DORA data; human error in manual deployments is well documented.

claims.text: An automated test is an investment that permanently prevents the class of problem it checks.
claims.note: Regression tests do prevent recurrence, but suites also incur maintenance and decay, which the claim ignores.

claims.text: Adopting continuous delivery shifts development effort from branch merging and support to new features and lowers cost per product.
claims.note: The HP LaserJet case documents this, but it is one firm with concurrent changes and no control.

claims.text: A continuous delivery pipeline gives regulated environments end-to-end traceability as a side effect.
claims.note: Pipelines do record provenance, but 'only way' is overstated since traditional change management also provides audit trails.

claims.text: Small functions are easier to read and modify but harder to debug, so the evidence for them is mixed.
claims.note: A few small studies point this way; the evidence base is too thin to call it settled.

claims.text: Abbreviated identifiers are no harder to debug than full-word identifiers.
claims.note: Scanniello et al. found no difference for debugging, but other comprehension studies found full words help, so results conflict.

claims.text: Code smells mark where bugs are likely, but fixing the smells does not remove the bugs.
claims.note: Supported by mining studies of long-lived projects; effects vary by smell type.

claims.text: Large-scale repository studies claiming some languages produce fewer bugs did not survive replication.
claims.note: Independent repetition and reanalysis of Ray et al.'s 729-project study: mislabelled TypeScript files, duplicated bitcoin forks, 36% false-positive bug labels and no multiple-testing correction; only 4 of the 11 claimed language-defect associations survive and even those have exceedingly small effect sizes.

claims.text: Test-driven development produces no better quality or productivity than other disciplined testing approaches.
claims.note: Blind-analysis crossover replication with 21 graduate students found no difference between TDD and incremental test-last in tests written (p=1.00), external quality (p=.82) or productivity (p=.82), with negligible effect sizes, confirming the Oulu baseline experiment.

claims.text: Pair programming shows little measurable effect on defects or productivity in controlled studies.
claims.note: Hannay et al.'s meta-analysis found small quality gains and effort increases with high heterogeneity.

claims.text: Code review catches most of the defects in reviewed code.
claims.note: Inspection studies report high detection rates under limited review rates; modern lightweight review finds fewer.

claims.text: Most code review findings are maintainability improvements rather than functional bugs.
claims.note: Card sort of 570 Microsoft review comments: code improvement (readability, dead code, practices) is the largest category at 29%, defects only fourth at 14%, and 65 of 78 defect comments are small logic slips rather than design or security issues.

claims.text: Sleep, stress and hours worked affect output more than any technical practice.
claims.note: Fatigue effects are large and robust, but no study directly compares them against technical practices on the same scale.

claims.text: Open-plan offices are adopted mainly because they cut real-estate cost per worker.
claims.note: Cost is a commonly cited motive alongside collaboration goals, but motives are not measured.

claims.text: How much to invest in tests depends on required feedback frequency, fidelity, overhead and the expected lifespan of the code.
claims.note: A decision framework rather than a measurable claim.

claims.text: Automated tests give little feedback on whether a feature serves users or whether the codebase is healthy.
claims.note: Tests check specified behaviour; user value and design health need other feedback, though some tests target design.

claims.text: Confidence from programmer-written tests led many teams to drop QA and ship lower quality.
claims.note: Anecdotal; some companies did cut QA, but no study links this to measured quality loss.

claims.text: Strict TDD, which forbids production code without a failing test, is incompatible with trading off coverage by criticality.
claims.note: A logical argument about methodology consistency rather than a measurable outcome.

claims.text: Programmers taking responsibility for quality was a large improvement over throwing code over the wall to QA.
claims.note: Widely agreed from experience; little direct measurement comparing the two arrangements.

claims.text: Automating scripted QA checks lets teams get release answers in hours instead of weeks.
claims.note: Test automation shortens feedback cycles in DORA and industrial reports; the gain depends on suite quality.

claims.text: Being on call for production teaches developers which tests and feedback loops they are missing.
claims.note: A reasonable mechanism consistent with DevOps practice; not measured.

claims.text: Agile has been turned from an adjective into a product sold through certification, training and consultancy, losing the original values
claims.note: A historical and framing claim about an industry, not a measurable outcome.

claims.text: No software development rule is universal; every practice only works in a context
claims.note: The review concludes agile methods are not necessarily the best choice for large projects, found XP hard to introduce in a complex organisation yet easy elsewhere, and advises practitioners to compare their project's characteristics with each method's required characteristics.

claims.text: Once a developer has internalised test-driven design thinking, the design benefit remains even if the tests are no longer written first
claims.note: Self-reported by experienced practitioners; no study separates the design effect of TDD from the habit it builds.

claims.text: Testing advocacy has become a dogma that shames developers who do not follow it
claims.note: A claim about community culture and tone, not a measurable effect.

claims.text: Scaled agile frameworks appeal to large organisations because they look complex, not because they are shown to work
claims.note: No controlled evidence either way on SAFe-style frameworks; adopter surveys are mixed and self-reported.

claims.text: A good design is one that is easier to change than a bad design, and every design principle follows from that
claims.note: A definition and design heuristic rather than a prediction.

claims.text: Agility means taking a small step, evaluating the result and repeating, rather than following a prescribed method
claims.note: Short, uniform development cycles were the factors associated with better quality and productivity while the prescribed test-first order was not, supporting small steps over rule-following, but only for short-term workshop tasks by 39 professionals.

claims.text: Short certification courses produce practitioners who follow prescribed steps without understanding why
claims.note: Plausible and consistent with cargo-cult reports, but no study links certification length to team outcomes.

claims.text: Some programmers are vastly more productive than their typical peers
claims.note: Interpersonal work time differences are real and larger than most experimental effects, but the slowest-to-fastest-quarter ratio is rarely above 4 and the Grant/Sackman 28:1 figure (really 14:1) looks like an outlier; the author cautions that student populations may understate practical variability.

claims.text: Rapid individual output often comes at the cost of maintainability that the rest of the team pays for
claims.note: Widely reported anecdotally; no study measures downstream debt created by high-output individuals.

claims.text: Most software effort goes into understanding, maintaining, extending and operating code rather than writing it
claims.note: Maintenance is generally estimated to consume well over half of lifecycle effort, though the exact figures are poorly sourced.

claims.text: Excellence in engineering takes different forms; a few well-judged lines can be worth more than high-volume output
claims.note: A values statement about what counts as excellence.

claims.text: A pair finishes a task faster than one person but spends more total person-hours on it
claims.note: Meta-analysis finds pairs cut elapsed time but raise total effort; the sixty-percent figure comes from small student studies.

claims.text: Pairing pays off on novel, hard work and wastes effort on routine or repetitive tasks
claims.note: Meta-analysis finds pairing's benefit concentrated on complex tasks, consistent with this.

claims.text: Skill mismatch within a pair matters little; every expert and novice combination produces value
claims.note: Experiments find novice pairs gain most and expert pairs least; all combinations show some benefit.

claims.text: Many widely repeated software engineering facts trace back to sources that are missing, measure something else, or are methodologically flawed
claims.note: One documented instance: the famous 28:1 programmer variability figure is wrong (two methodological mistakes, correct value 14:1), rests on 12 subjects, was published in an obscure journal, and kept being quoted after Dickey debunked it in 1981.

claims.text: The cone of uncertainty in estimation has no empirical basis
claims.note: Boehm presented it as a notional diagram; later project data did not show estimates narrowing as the cone predicts.

claims.text: Story-point velocity is only stable while the team is stable; adding or removing people changes it
claims.note: Consistent with Brooks's law and observed velocity volatility after staffing changes, though mostly practitioner data.

claims.text: Story points forecast delivery only on average across several iterations, never for a single sprint
claims.note: Aggregate forecasting improves with history; per-sprint accuracy is poor in most reported data.

claims.text: Story-point estimation and sprint commitment are alternative ways to fill an iteration, not complements
claims.note: A definitional stance on process design.

claims.text: Automated formatting and static analysis before review let reviewers focus on design and maintainability
claims.note: Google's and Mozilla's review studies both find static analysis integration reduces trivial comments.

claims.text: Code review is a major channel for learning and knowledge transfer, especially for newcomers
claims.note: Surveys at Microsoft and Google rank knowledge transfer among the top benefits of review.

claims.text: Extensive automated pre-submit checks catch most breaking changes before they are merged
claims.note: Pre-submit CI catches many regressions, but the share depends on test coverage; the figure is a personal estimate.

claims.text: Newly joined engineers receive the most review comments, and the count falls with tenure
claims.note: Log analysis of ~9M Google changes: authors who started within the past year receive more than twice as many reviewer comments per change, and the average falls steadily over the first five years of tenure (Figure 2).

claims.text: Overly harsh or demanding reviews discourage future contributions
claims.note: Studies of open-source projects link toxic review comments to contributor drop-off; in-company data is thin.

claims.text: Tests serve as precise, unambiguous low-level documentation of the system
claims.note: Tests document behaviour but are hard to navigate as documentation; evidence is practitioner opinion.

claims.text: GUI-driven integration tests cannot reach a large fraction of code such as error handling and edge cases
claims.note: Coverage from end-to-end tests is typically well below unit-level coverage; the 'bit more than half' figure is a guess.

claims.text: Keeping code clean enough to keep development fast is worth more than the cost of building a trustworthy test suite
claims.note: A cost-benefit judgment with no agreed way to measure either side.

claims.text: Focused and collaborative work need different physical spaces
claims.note: Removing all spatial boundaries cut face-to-face collaboration about 70%, and the authors tie this to Kao and Couzin's finding that intermediate rather than maximal openness maximises collective intelligence; supports that fully open space hurts both kinds of work but does not test separate spaces.

claims.text: Workspace design is a fundamental part of how a company takes care of its people
claims.note: A values statement.

claims.text: The claim that defect fix cost rises exponentially by lifecycle phase has no verifiable measurement behind it
claims.note: Boehm's original data exists but is thinner than the derived charts; modern iterative projects show much flatter curves.

claims.text: Software project failure rates and crisis figures are exaggerated and often based on opinion surveys
claims.note: Standish CHAOS figures are widely criticised; failure definitions vary so much that no robust rate exists.

claims.text: Software folklore spreads because the field is fashion-driven and debunking costs more effort than asserting
claims.note: Uncovering the flaws in one well-regarded study took the reproduction team about 5 person-months (over 6 months elapsed), while the original result had already spread through 119 citations, most repeating it as a causal effect; supports the asymmetry between asserting and debunking, says nothing about fashion.

claims.text: Easy-to-repeat claims act as curiosity stoppers that prevent investigating what actually makes projects succeed
claims.note: A framing claim about how folklore affects inquiry.

claims.text: Measuring software work in man-months is misleading because adding people does not add proportional progress
claims.note: Lego-team experiment: four-person teams took 53 minutes total versus 36 for two-person teams on the same task and underestimated more (75% vs 55% overrun), and IT projects with more people overrun more often; a workforce twice as large delivers less than twice the output.

claims.text: Apparent standout productivity can reflect tenure, project selection, information hoarding or credit-taking rather than skill
claims.note: Plausible confounders; no study separates them from genuine skill differences.

claims.text: Version control and code review let junior engineers write production code safely, replacing hierarchical chief-programmer teams
claims.note: Review and version control do gate bad code, but flatter teams also reflect cheaper compute; no causal study.

claims.text: Preferring runtime polymorphism over switch statements makes code slower by forcing pointer indirection and hiding the code path from the compiler
claims.note: Reproducible on this microbenchmark; the gain in real programs depends on how much time hot loops spend in dispatch.

claims.text: Fusing data layout with the operation in table-driven, data-oriented code can be an order of magnitude faster than encapsulated class hierarchies
claims.note: Well-known data-oriented design result for compute-bound loops; most application code is not compute-bound.

claims.text: Following clean-code structure rules can cost performance equivalent to a decade or more of hardware improvement
claims.note: Holds for the toy benchmark; in typical applications I/O, allocation and network dominate so the end-to-end cost is far smaller.

claims.text: The performance penalty of class-hierarchy designs grows as the problem gets more complex
claims.note: Adding a second virtual call widened the gap here, but this is one extra property on a toy problem.

claims.text: Avoiding repeated code does not conflict with writing fast code
claims.note: Reasonable in general; some performance work deliberately duplicates code paths for specialisation.

claims.text: Code organised by operation rather than by type makes shared patterns visible and easier to simplify
claims.note: A design-perception claim with no agreed measure.

claims.text: Clean-code rules were adopted for maintainability without evidence that they deliver it
claims.note: Evidence that small functions or polymorphism improve maintainability is thin and mixed; readability studies are mostly small.

claims.text: Controlled studies find at most small effects of static typing on productivity or defect rates
claims.note: Repeated-measures ANOVA gave significant, medium-to-large effects of language on development time in both rounds (partial eta-squared .275 and .246) with a strong task-language interaction; the exploratory measures showed 35-69 percent of variance in test runs and file switches explained by the type system in the second round, which is not a small effect, though confined to small tasks.

claims.text: Differences between individual programmers dwarf differences between languages in experiments
claims.note: Across 80 programs the within-language bad/good ratios for time, length, memory and run time were on average about as large as or larger than the between-language differences, which supports the direction but not 'dwarf', since scripts still took half the time of C/C++/Java.

claims.text: Type annotations help developers mainly by acting as documentation when using unfamiliar APIs
claims.note: The exploratory data show static types cut file switches on class-identification tasks, which the authors interpret as annotations guiding developers to the right API without searching, but they cannot separate annotation from checking and type-error fixing benefited at least as strongly.

claims.text: Retrofitting static types onto dynamically typed programs finds only a small fraction of their bugs
claims.note: Flow and TypeScript each detect 60 of 400 sampled public JavaScript bugs (15%, 95% CI 11.5-18.5%), so retrofitted types find a minority of bugs, but the authors stress this is a lower bound (public bugs only, two weak type systems, non-expert annotators) and an engineering manager called a 10% reduction a no-brainer.

claims.text: Existing type-system studies do not cover experienced programmers, large codebases or modern typed languages
claims.note: The threats section concedes mostly student subjects, small tasks without complex control flow in a bare text editor, and Java as a type system 'not known for being the most expressive'; the related-work survey lists only similar small experiments, matching all three gaps in the claim.

claims.text: Type-system studies are cherry-picked to confirm whichever side one already holds
claims.note: The original study's static-typing and functional-language results drew the most attention because they confirmed commonly held beliefs, and of 30 citing papers that discussed the results, 26 restated the correlations as causal effects; confirmation-driven over-reading of one study rather than cherry-picking across studies.

claims.text: Reaching the top few percent in most activities mainly requires correcting basic, observable mistakes rather than talent
claims.note: Consistent with deliberate-practice findings, but the game evidence is observational and self-selected.

claims.text: Getting feedback on one's own work yields large improvements because almost no practitioners seek any
claims.note: Coaching and feedback effects are robust in education research; the 'almost no one' part is anecdotal.

claims.text: Tracking where programming time actually goes reveals large, fixable waste that self-perception misses
claims.note: Self-report of time use is known to be inaccurate; the twofold gain is a single self-estimate.

claims.text: Skilled coaching beats peer or self feedback for improving at a skill
claims.note: Tutoring and expert coaching show large effects in education meta-analyses.

claims.text: Independent gut estimates from experienced practitioners converge and are reasonably accurate at project scale
claims.note: Expert judgment matches formal models in estimation research, but these are a handful of successful anecdotes.

claims.text: Detailed story-by-story estimation inflates the total because micro-planning is fractal
claims.note: Decomposition yields higher totals because small tasks are less underestimated (magnitude effect); in two office-task experiments decomposed sums were 9-10% too high vs 2-5% for whole-task estimates, and a software study found decomposed estimates higher but less accurate. The mechanism is magnitude bias, not fractal micro-planning.

claims.text: Estimating individual stories adds little because the biggest risks are cross-cutting unknowns no single story captures
claims.note: Plausible and consistent with project post-mortems, but no comparative measurement.

claims.text: Revealing estimates simultaneously prevents the first number spoken from anchoring the rest
claims.note: Planning poker's simultaneous reveal is described as keeping initial estimates independent and unanchored, and a field study found it cut median estimation error from 50% to 33%; combinations of independent predictions beat ones influenced by each other.

claims.text: An estimate is better framed as an investment decision than as a contract
claims.note: Bid, planned effort and most-likely effort have conflicting goals, and software estimators frequently do not distinguish them, which the review argues hinders realistic estimates; the investment-decision framing itself is not tested.

claims.text: Sometimes the honest estimate is that size cannot be known until specific unknowns are investigated
claims.note: When no relevant historical data exist the recommended method is to start the work and extrapolate from the first stage, which supports deferring the estimate until unknowns are probed, though the book still expects a prediction before starting.

claims.text: Merge tools cannot detect functional conflicts between independently developed features; only integrating and testing can
claims.note: Semantic conflicts are invisible to textual merge; this is the standard rationale for CI.

claims.text: Choosing which features to release after integration testing means shipping a combination that was never tested
claims.note: Logically sound; the size of the risk depends on how coupled the features are.

claims.text: Trunk-based development with feature toggles is simpler for most teams than disciplined branch-per-feature
claims.note: Survey data favours trunk-based teams, but 'simpler' is a judgment and toggles carry their own cost.

claims.text: Keeping a branch per feature lets a finished feature be pulled before release, which trunk-based development cannot do
claims.note: True without toggles; feature flags give trunk-based teams the same ability at some complexity cost.

claims.text: Feature toggles are a hack and a source of errors that proper branch-per-feature avoids
claims.note: Toggle debt and misconfiguration incidents are real, but branches trade them for merge risk; no comparison exists.

claims.text: Generic repository abstractions over an ORM lead to N+1 queries and joining in application memory
claims.note: A commonly documented .NET anti-pattern; the problem is the abstraction's inflexibility rather than inevitability.

claims.text: Skipping architecture review in a project's first weeks locks in decisions that take years to undo
claims.note: Early structural decisions are the costliest to reverse, though the exponential defect-cost curve behind this is overstated.

claims.text: Giving requirements without having the engineer explain them back leads to them being silently ignored
claims.note: Read-back is standard in safety-critical communication; software evidence is anecdotal.

claims.text: AI coding tools reproduce a codebase's existing anti-patterns unless a new pattern is established first
claims.note: Consistent with how code models condition on context; measured mainly in practitioner reports.

claims.text: End-to-end browser tests are brittle but the fastest way to get coverage from zero on a legacy system
claims.note: Matches the test-pyramid rationale; brittleness of UI tests is well documented.

claims.text: Writing down architecture decisions and their reasoning helps both humans and AI tools work on a codebase
claims.note: ADRs are widely adopted; the benefit is reported, not measured.

claims.text: Reviewing code synchronously at commit time rather than asynchronously reduces merge delay and conflicts
claims.note: The delay-to-conflict link is well supported; whether synchronous review is practical at scale is less clear.

claims.text: Running the automated test suite before every commit keeps trunk releasable
claims.note: Standard CI mechanism; effectiveness depends on suite coverage and speed.

claims.text: Trunk-based development requires developers to learn to work in small batches, which many find hard and resist
claims.note: Adoption reports consistently cite resistance; the magnitude is anecdotal.

claims.text: Programs are rarely inherently I/O bound; chatty serial chains of dependent requests make them look I/O bound
claims.note: Waterfall request chains are a well-documented cause of slow web apps, but large-data workloads genuinely are bounded by storage and network even when well structured.

claims.text: Faster, more responsive software measurably increases user engagement and revenue
claims.note: Published latency experiments at Amazon, Google and others consistently show engagement and conversion dropping with added delay, though 'conclusive' overstates how far the effect generalises to internal tools.

claims.text: Hiding implementation details behind layers of abstraction makes it harder to find why code misbehaves because every layer must be dug through
claims.note: Information hiding has evidence for isolating change, and indirection is also known to hurt comprehension; which dominates for debugging has not been measured.

claims.text: The readability gains credited to class hierarchies come from cleaning up messy code, which well-named procedural code achieves equally well
claims.note: Comprehension experiments find naming and structure matter more than paradigm, but no study compares a tidy procedural version against a hierarchy on the same task.

claims.text: Switch-based code is easier to optimise later than a class hierarchy because all cases are visible in one place
claims.note: Merging cases into branch-free or vectorised code is standard practice and needs the cases in one place, but this is a specialist optimisation path rather than a general maintenance cost.

claims.text: Lines of code per feature is a useful objective proxy for code that reads like what it does and stays easy to modify
claims.note: Lines of code predict defects and effort about as well as any complexity metric, but minimising it can also produce dense, cryptic code.

claims.text: The 'premature optimisation' quote is misapplied as licence to ignore performance during design when it only warned against early micro-level hand tuning
claims.note: The full Knuth passage explicitly says not to pass up the critical few percent and concerns small-scale efficiencies, not architecture.

claims.text: Developer-time savings claimed from ignoring performance are erased by later ground-up performance rewrites
claims.note: Several large companies have published performance-driven rewrites, but the examples are survivors whose slow first version reached market, so the net accounting is unknown.

claims.text: A performance trade-off only counts as a trade-off if the cost was measured; otherwise it is an excuse
claims.note: This is a framing about what deserves the word trade-off rather than a testable prediction.

claims.text: Performance must be designed in from the start because hotspot optimisation cannot fix serial dependency chains and poor data layout later
claims.note: Architectural choices like synchronous call chains are expensive to undo, but profiling-driven fixes resolve many real slowdowns without redesign.

claims.text: Decomposing code into very small methods can go too far, producing shallow interfaces and entangled methods that are harder to read than one longer method
claims.note: Controlled studies find no comprehension gain from splitting code into very small methods, though none establishes where the optimum lies.

claims.text: Modular decomposition behind simple interfaces reduces the information a programmer must hold in mind at once
claims.note: Working-memory limits are well established and information hiding has long-standing empirical support for change isolation.

claims.text: Treating comments as failures leads to under-documented code, and missing comments cost far more time than incorrect ones
claims.note: Comprehension experiments show well-placed comments help readers, but stale-comment costs are real and the cost ratio is one practitioner's estimate.

claims.text: For most software, conserving programmer time matters more than conserving CPU cycles, so readability-first practices pay off
claims.note: Much business software is not CPU-bound and developer salaries dominate costs, but published latency experiments show slowness has measurable revenue costs too.

claims.text: Choosing the right algorithm improves efficiency by many orders of magnitude while cycle-level tuning gives about one
claims.note: Asymptotic improvements dominate constant-factor ones on large inputs, though for fixed-size hot loops constant factors are all that remain.

claims.text: Clean Code teaching gives performance almost no attention, so its audience learns to ignore it
claims.note: The author conceded the point about his own lecture series; whether audiences actually absorb a disregard for performance is not measured.

claims.text: Interactive and visual behaviour such as GUIs and game feel cannot practically be test-driven because the correct answer is not known up front
claims.note: Both debaters and the game industry agree; snapshot and replay testing cover regressions but not the initial judgement of correctness.

claims.text: Polymorphism makes adding new types easy while switch statements make adding new operations easy; neither is a free win
claims.note: This is the well-known expression problem; the two designs are mirror images for the two kinds of extension.

claims.text: Dependency inversion via polymorphism protects high-level policy from recompilation and redeployment when low-level details change
claims.note: The mechanism is real, but link-time binding through opaque pointers gives the same isolation, so the benefit specific to runtime polymorphism is mainly plugins and frameworks.

claims.text: Very small changes can be worse than mid-sized ones because their implications are hidden and they are reverted more often
claims.note: One vendor dataset shows higher revert rates under ten lines, plausibly from config changes; the pattern has not been replicated.

claims.text: Refactorings should be in separate changes from feature work and bug fixes so reviewers can understand each
claims.note: Tangled changes are shown to confuse both reviewers and defect analysis, though no study measures the review-quality gain directly.

claims.text: Every change that adds or alters logic should ship with its tests in the same change
claims.note: Widely adopted policy, but no study compares co-committed tests against tests landed separately.

claims.text: Almost any large change can be decomposed into a series of small ones by an author who practises it
claims.note: Stacking and vertical slicing work for most feature work, but generated code, large migrations and some refactors resist splitting.

claims.text: Very large changes merge faster and are reverted less than mid-sized ones, likely because they are generated or refactor-only
claims.note: The pattern appears in one dataset and the explanation is the author's guess; rubber-stamping would also hide defects rather than prevent them.

claims.text: Observed benefits of small PRs are partly selection: teams already practising trunk-based development make smaller PRs
claims.note: The author flags the confound; no study randomises PR size, so some of the correlation is team maturity.

claims.text: Unit tests that never fail in version control still earn their keep because they fail transiently during development and are fixed before commit
claims.note: Local failures are invisible to repository history so 'never failed' undercounts value, but maintenance cost is real and tests that never fail even locally may be low value.

claims.text: Tests breaking during refactoring is a minor cost in practice
claims.note: Test co-evolution studies show test maintenance is a real and recurring effort, heavily dependent on how mock-heavy and implementation-coupled the tests are.

claims.text: The impossibility of exhaustively testing a program's state space applies to integration tests as much as unit tests
claims.note: Both are samples, but a system-level test exercises many units per case, so the argument cuts differently per test.

claims.text: Unit tests make it easy to set up edge-case contexts that are hard to reproduce in the full system
claims.note: Near-definitional and borne out by practice; error-handling paths in particular are hard to trigger end to end.

claims.text: Runtime assertions complement but cannot replace unit tests because an assertion failure is still a production failure
claims.note: Assertions do catch what tests missed but after shipping; the two find overlapping faults at different costs.

claims.text: Combining unit and integration tests catches more than integration tests alone
claims.note: Different test levels find different fault classes, but no study quantifies the marginal catch of adding unit tests to a good integration suite.

claims.text: Best practices are inherited from what the most successful programmers do, which cannot distinguish good techniques from bad ones they succeed despite
claims.note: The logic holds and practice adoption is visibly driven by prominent advocates, but how much of practice folklore actually originates this way is not measured.

claims.text: Making expert advocates argue opposing positions publicly is a partial substitute for missing research
claims.note: A preference about discourse rather than a prediction that could be checked.

claims.text: The most damaging software faults are design flaws rather than coding slips
claims.note: Classic industrial fault studies attribute the costliest defects to requirements and design, but the split depends heavily on how faults are categorised.

claims.text: Simple tests of error-handling paths could prevent most catastrophic failures in distributed systems
claims.note: A study of production outages in major distributed systems found most catastrophic failures stemmed from trivially testable error-handling bugs.

claims.text: Lines of code predict defects about as well as any complexity metric
claims.note: Studies of large codebases find most complexity metrics are strongly correlated with size and add little predictive power.

claims.text: Organisational structure metrics predict defect-prone components better than code metrics
claims.note: On 3,404 Windows Vista binaries (50M+ LOC, 50 random splits), eight organizational metrics predict failure-prone binaries with 86.2% precision and 84.0% recall versus 78.6/79.9 for churn, 79.3/66.0 for complexity, 74.4/69.9 for dependencies, 83.8/54.4 for coverage and 73.8/62.9 for pre-release bugs; single system.

claims.text: Knowledge-worker productivity cannot be measured reliably, so hours-versus-output conclusions rest on analogies from other industries
