claims.note: Lines of code and function points are widely criticised as proxies and no accepted output measure exists for programmers.

claims.text: Complex mental work degrades faster under fatigue than physical work, so knowledge workers lose more to long hours than manual workers
claims.note: Sleep research shows higher-order cognition is most sensitive to sleep loss, but the inference that programmers lose more total output than factory workers is unmeasured.

claims.text: Managers impose crunch to signal effort rather than because it works
claims.note: Asks why employers kept long hours when shorter hours gave the same output and offers Hicks's answer that it 'never entered the heads of most employers' that hours could be cut without losing output; consistent with crunch not working, but attributes it to ignorance rather than effort signalling.

claims.text: Much delivered functionality is rarely or never used, so working through a prioritised backlog wastes effort compared with selecting high-impact items
claims.note: The widely cited 64% figure comes from a small Standish sample; feature usage is skewed but the magnitude is unknown.

claims.text: Scope growth during a project is mostly value discovered while building, and following the original plan discards it
claims.note: Requirements do emerge during development, but scope creep also includes gold-plating and unmanaged change, so treating all of it as value is optimistic.

claims.text: Estimation techniques were developed for other industries and may not fit software
claims.note: Unlike most studied professions where models beat experts, software expert estimates match or beat models because case-specific knowledge matters more and software size-effort models perform worse, so results from other domains transfer imperfectly.

claims.text: Technical debt consumes a substantial fraction of developers' working time
claims.note: Besker et al. surveys report roughly a quarter of time self-reported as wasted, but the figures are self-reported and vary widely.

claims.text: Code in unhealthy files has many times more defects and takes several times longer to change than healthy code
claims.note: Across 30,737 files in 39 proprietary codebases, Alert (low Code Health) files had 15x the Jira defects of Healthy files and issues took 124% (about 2.2x) longer on average, so 'many times more defects' holds but 'several times longer' overstates the average time effect; observational, CodeScene-customer sample, vendor-authored, causality direction acknowledged as open.

claims.text: Low-quality code makes delivery times unpredictable, not just slower
claims.note: The maximum Time-in-Development per file was 9x longer in Alert code than Healthy code (large effect, Cohen's d 0.96) and already 2x in Warning code, with much higher variance, which the authors read as lower predictability of task completion; correlational, single tool vendor's customer base.

claims.text: Technical debt lowers developer happiness and drives attrition
claims.note: Graziotin and others link bad code to frustration and lower productivity; attrition effects are anecdotal.

claims.text: Prioritising refactoring by hotspots, where change frequency meets low code health, targets the debt with the highest interest
claims.note: Change-frequency weighting is a sensible proxy supported by defect-prediction research, but comparative outcome data is limited to vendor case studies.

claims.text: Code quality is tolerated as waste because it is invisible to non-technical stakeholders
claims.note: The motivation section relays that the business impact of code quality is vague, managers in a 15-organisation study would not fund refactoring because benefits were unclear, there are no code-quality KPIs comparable to financial ones, and only 10% of 1,831 surveyed said their business manager managed TD; all cited from other studies rather than measured here.

claims.text: Splitting services too finely raises inter-service dependencies and coordination so total cost rises again rather than falling
claims.note: Structured Design's inter/intra-module cost curve and reports of shotgun surgery across many services support this; no controlled measurement.

claims.text: Service boundaries are usually wrong on the first attempt because the domain is not yet understood, so systems built as microservices from scratch tend to end in trouble
claims.note: Consistent practitioner anecdote from Fowler, Newman and others, but anecdotes suffer selection bias.

claims.text: Keeping modules in one process with enforced boundaries gets most of the modularity benefit without the distribution cost
claims.note: Modular monolith reports from Shopify and Prime Video are positive, but in-process boundaries are known to erode without tooling.

claims.text: Moving functionality across service boundaries is far harder than refactoring inside one process
claims.note: No IDE-level refactoring crosses process or API boundaries; coordinated deploys and versioning are required.

claims.text: Headlines about big companies abandoning microservices usually describe one team consolidating a few components
claims.note: The Prime Video post concerned one team's service; Amazon overall remained service-based.

claims.text: Creating services by which team is free rather than by domain seams produces fragmented systems
claims.note: Conway's-law reasoning and anecdote; no measured outcome data.

claims.text: Service boundaries must be repartitioned continually as the business changes, so owning microservices is never finished
claims.note: Domain drift is real; whether it demands service repartitioning rather than internal change depends on granularity.

claims.text: 'Micro' should mean replaceable, not few lines of code
claims.note: Definitional.

claims.text: Estimation is a learnable skill: recording estimates and comparing them to outcomes calibrates future estimates
claims.note: Independent studies of the Personal Software Process, which records estimates and analyses deviations from actuals, found no improvement in estimation accuracy, and a feedback-and-lessons-learned programme likewise produced none versus untrained controls.

claims.text: Giving accurate timelines builds trust and is required to advance beyond senior engineering roles
claims.note: Career advice.

claims.text: Avoiding estimates improves planning conversations, but business commitments still sometimes require a time-based estimate
claims.note: Reasonable synthesis; practitioner consensus rather than measured.

claims.text: Legacy code results from technical neglect, the failure to keep refactoring, rather than from technical debt itself
claims.note: A reframing consistent with debt-interest models but not separately testable.

claims.text: Automated refactoring tools have existed for decades yet legacy code persists, so the obstacle is mindset not tooling
claims.note: Tool-usage studies show refactoring tools are underused, which supports the mindset explanation.

claims.text: Never trust a test you have not seen fail
claims.note: Mutation testing routinely finds tests that cannot fail; seeing the red state is the standard guard.

claims.text: Refactoring in small behaviour-preserving steps with tests or compiler checks at each step avoids the big-bang breakage trap
claims.note: Core of Fowler's refactoring method; supported by practitioner evidence more than experiments.

claims.text: In refactoring-oriented development most commits reposition code so that the final feature addition is a trivial change
claims.note: Describes a workflow; the ratio is one practitioner's anecdote.

claims.text: Refactor a problem on its own terms before migrating it to a different paradigm
claims.note: Methodological preference.

claims.text: Programming productivity has no physical ceiling, so hard work can make anyone a 10x engineer
claims.note: Weekly output of munitions workers reached a maximum near 63 h and the marginal product of further hours was negative, so a ceiling on what extra hours can buy exists at least for physical piece work; programming was not studied.

claims.text: Continuous delivery does not require microservices; monoliths can be deployed continuously
claims.note: Facebook, Etsy, Shopify and GitHub have all deployed monoliths many times a day.

claims.text: Hype drives teams to adopt microservices they do not need, adding cost and risk
claims.note: Microservice envy is widely reported; its magnitude is unmeasured.

claims.text: Decomposing a monolith only works if it already has a reasonably modular design; tangled monoliths just produce a mess
claims.note: Consistent with migration case studies, though some decompositions of tangled code succeeded with heavy investment.

claims.text: Pairing all day is unsustainable because sustained joint focus is exhausting
claims.note: Self-reported fatigue is consistent across pairing studies; no measured limit.

claims.text: After-the-fact code review is weaker than pairing because reviewers skim, defer to the author and resist rework already invested
claims.note: Microsoft studies show reviews catch fewer defects than expected, but head-to-head comparisons with pairing are lacking.

claims.text: Juniors who always pair can lose confidence and miss learning to solve problems alone
claims.note: Plausible and reported, though novice studies mostly show pairing helps juniors.

claims.text: Power dynamics such as seniority or gender distort pairing when one person dominates the keyboard or dismisses suggestions
claims.note: Qualitative studies document the dynamic; its effect on outcomes is unmeasured.

claims.text: Pairing limits team work in progress, which improves flow
claims.note: WIP limits improve flow in Kanban studies; attributing that to pairing is inference.

claims.text: Pairing's value cannot be proven scientifically because development output is too hard to measure, so teams must try it themselves
claims.note: The review describes research on particular practices like pair programming as at an intermediate or even mature state, and cites an earlier review calling pair programming supported by a well-established research stream; the evidence may be mixed, but the authors treat it as a scientifically studiable question, not an unmeasurable one.

claims.text: Rote, repetitive code is a design smell, and pairing helps find the missing abstraction
claims.note: Plausible; no evidence.

claims.text: Pair programming is an XP practice, not a requirement of agile
claims.note: The review's table of agile methods lists pair programming among XP's twelve practices, while the descriptions of Scrum, Crystal, DSDM, FDD and Lean and the agile manifesto's four values make no mention of it.

claims.text: Debt is prudent when taken deliberately to ship sooner with small interest, and reckless when taken without understanding its cost
claims.note: Classification framework.

claims.text: Even excellent teams accumulate inadvertent debt because the right design is only learned by building the system
claims.note: Matches design-emergence research and practitioner consensus; not experimentally tested.

claims.text: The debt metaphor helps explain design problems to non-technical stakeholders
claims.note: Communication framing.

claims.text: Rotating the driver every few minutes keeps every team member engaged
claims.note: Engagement is self-reported; no comparative data.

claims.text: In a mob the group coaches a less-skilled driver on the spot, raising everyone's skills
claims.note: Case reports from Hunter Industries and others are positive; no controlled studies.

claims.text: A rewrite is viable when the codebase is small, the product is not the main revenue source and there is a compelling business case
claims.note: Derived from a handful of personal cases; plausible conditions with no broader data.

claims.text: Rewrite duration grows faster than linearly with codebase size and complexity, making estimates for large rewrites unreliable
claims.note: Consistent with overrun data showing large projects overrun most, though the exponential form is hand-waved.

claims.text: Tech debt and distaste for old code alone are not a sufficient reason to rewrite a large successful product
claims.note: Consistent with Spolsky and with rewrite failure cases; opinion-based.

claims.text: Microservices' independent scaling and fault isolation pay off at very large scale where downtime is costly
claims.note: Netflix and Amazon cases support it; there is no evidence about where the threshold lies.

claims.text: No single architecture suits every scale, so architecture should be revisited with each order of magnitude of growth
claims.note: Heuristic.

claims.text: A single-process design suits long-running compute jobs and predictable traffic better than serverless functions
claims.note: Lambda pricing and duration limits make this true for sustained workloads; Cockcroft's advice is widely echoed.

claims.text: Microservices speed time to market
claims.note: Independent deploys can speed large organisations, but monolith-first advocates argue the opposite for small teams; no comparative data.

claims.text: Programming needs blocks of at least half a day, so a single mid-block meeting destroys the block
claims.note: Interruption studies by Mark and Parnin show substantial resumption cost; the half-day unit is unmeasured.

claims.text: Knowing a block will be interrupted deters starting ambitious work, so a meeting costs more than its duration
claims.note: Plausible anticipatory effect; self-report only.

claims.text: Clustering meetings at the end of the day preserves uninterrupted maker time
claims.note: Follows from interruption cost; no outcome data.

claims.text: Managers and makers run on different schedules, and conflict arises when hourly manager slots are imposed on makers
claims.note: Framing.

claims.text: Serverless lets small teams ship without managing infrastructure and often within free tiers
claims.note: True for low, bursty traffic; costs and limits bite at sustained load, as the same video's Prime Video case shows.

claims.text: There are no solutions in cloud architecture, only trade-offs
claims.note: Aphorism.

claims.text: Functions should be extracted until each does one thing, meaning nothing further can be meaningfully extracted
claims.note: Smaller methods correlate with fewer defects up to a point, but studies find very small, deeply delegating methods hurt comprehension.

claims.text: Large functions are classes in disguise; extracting until stuck reveals hidden classes
claims.note: Extract Class from shared locals is a standard refactoring; 'every' overstates.

claims.text: Function-length rules such as fit on one screen came from historical terminal sizes, not evidence
claims.note: Historical framing.

claims.text: Story points began as renamed ideal days, meant only to decide how much work fits an iteration
claims.note: Historical account from a participant.

claims.text: Using story points to predict delivery dates is weak, and comparing teams by velocity or estimate accuracy is harmful
claims.note: Velocity is team-relative by construction; Goodhart effects on normalised points are widely reported.

claims.text: Tracking estimates against actuals shifts attention from delivering value to improving estimates
claims.note: A company that paid bonuses for estimate accuracy saw accuracy improve while productivity fell because managers padded estimates and absorbed the buffer; accountability raised accuracy mainly by adjusting work content and quality to fit the estimate.

claims.text: Slicing stories small enough to finish in about a day gives a smooth flow of value and removes most need for estimates
claims.note: Small batches improve flow in lean research; whether slicing fully replaces estimation is unproven.

claims.text: Frequent small releases deliver more value than big-bang releases whose dates keep receding
claims.note: DORA and lean batch-size evidence favour small frequent releases.

claims.text: Monoliths without enforced boundaries become so coupled that small changes have unexpected effects and newcomers need enormous context
claims.note: Coupling-defect and comprehension research supports it; Shopify's developer survey is a single case.

claims.text: Organising code by business domain rather than technical layer makes code and its owners easier to find
claims.note: Package-by-feature is widely recommended; the evidence is practitioner experience.

claims.text: Early in a system's life little design is needed; design investment should start when feature speed begins to slow
claims.note: Fowler's design stamina hypothesis is a hypothesis; consistent with debt-payoff reasoning.

claims.text: Adding public interfaces around modules without untangling the dependency graph just adds indirection and makes code harder to change
claims.note: Consistent with coupling research and Parnas-style modularity theory, but the evidence here is one organization's experience report.

claims.text: Modules can only be reasoned about or tested in isolation when the dependency graph between them is sparse and acyclic
claims.note: Follows from how dependencies propagate change; cyclic dependency metrics correlate with defect proneness in several empirical studies.

claims.text: Large architecture changes to an actively developed codebase succeed only by changing average developer behaviour, not by a central team's effort
claims.note: Plausible and matches other large-refactor reports, but it is an organizational observation without controlled evidence.

claims.text: Imposing uniform coding conventions adds learning and compliance friction without making hard design problems easier
claims.note: Rules have a cost, but consistency also has measured comprehension benefits, so the net effect depends on the rule.

claims.text: Static dependency analysis gives faster and more actionable boundary enforcement than tracing runtime calls
claims.note: Static reference analysis is cheap and deterministic; dynamic tracing depends on test coverage and is noisy, though it catches reflective calls static analysis misses.

claims.text: Large-scale architecture refactors stay in an incomplete intermediate state far longer than planned
claims.note: Widely reported across migration case studies, but it is experience-based rather than measured.

claims.text: Explicit module ownership makes whole-codebase chores like framework upgrades easier to distribute
claims.note: Ownership clarity is linked to lower defect rates in Microsoft's organizational-metrics studies, but the upgrade claim is a single report.

claims.text: A small team can maintain a large product across many platforms from a single integrated codebase
claims.note: Basecamp is a real existence proof, but a single company's experience does not show other approaches would have failed.

claims.text: Many small services make it easy for knowledge to silo so only one person understands each part
claims.note: Service ownership does concentrate knowledge by design; whether that is worse than monolith hotspots has not been measured.

claims.text: Extracting one slice with divergent performance needs as a separate service captures most of the scaling benefit without distributing the whole system
claims.note: Targeted extraction is a standard migration pattern and matches Shopify's and others' reports, but 'most of the benefit' is not quantified.

claims.text: Many teams that adopted microservices are retreating to monoliths
claims.note: There are prominent consolidation stories (Amazon Prime Video, Segment) but no survey establishes a net trend.

claims.text: Measured productivity gaps between programmers are mostly between competent and net-negative developers, not between good and great
claims.note: Re-analyses of the classic studies show best-to-worst ratios of ten or more but quartile ratios nearer two to four, so the gap depends on which tail you include.

claims.text: Slowing down to investigate a problem before coding reduces later cleanup
claims.note: Upfront understanding reduces rework in design studies, though the optimal amount varies and this is an archetype, not data.

claims.text: Deep expertise in a narrow domain can make an engineer vastly more productive there but less useful elsewhere
claims.note: Expertise is domain-specific per expertise research, though top engineers often transfer reasonably well.

claims.text: Reviewer effectiveness falls off after about an hour of continuous review
claims.note: Vigilance decrement is well established in general, but direct evidence for code review durations is thin and vendor-sourced.

claims.text: Checklists catch omission defects that unstructured review tends to miss
claims.note: Checklist-based reading experiments show modest gains over ad hoc reading; 'most effective' is overstated.

claims.text: Using code review metrics for performance evaluation makes developers hostile and game the process
claims.note: Goodhart effects are well documented for productivity metrics generally; direct evidence for review metrics is anecdotal.

claims.text: Knowing code will be reviewed makes developers write cleaner code even on unreviewed changes
claims.note: Accountability effects are plausible and reported by practitioners, but the spot-check figures come from one vendor study.

claims.text: Lightweight tool-assisted review finds as many defects as formal inspection in a fraction of the time
claims.note: Vendor data; independent studies (Bacchelli and Bird) find modern lightweight review catches fewer defects than expected, with most value in knowledge transfer.

claims.text: Desirable test properties trade off; making tests more predictive of production makes them slower
claims.note: Integration and end-to-end tests are consistently slower than unit tests while catching more realistic failures; the test-pyramid literature rests on this.

claims.text: Tests that are deterministic and independent of run order are more valuable because flaky results erode trust
claims.note: Flaky-test research at Google and in academia shows order dependence and nondeterminism waste developer time and cause ignored failures.

claims.text: A passing test suite should be sufficient evidence that code is ready for production
claims.note: An aspiration; in practice tests cannot cover all production conditions, which is why canaries and monitoring exist.

claims.text: Static and dynamic typing differ in when types are enforced, not in how many types a language has
claims.note: Standard type-theory framing; the 'unityped' view is a legitimate static lens but says nothing about dynamic type counts.

claims.text: Any sound static type system rejects some programs that would never fail at run time
claims.note: Follows from undecidability; every practical sound type system is incomplete.

claims.text: Encoding a dynamically typed program in a static type system bloats it with explicit checks the runtime would do implicitly
claims.note: True for naive sum-type encodings; gradual and inferred systems reduce but do not eliminate the annotation burden.

claims.text: Static analysis is unsound and incomplete, so it can augment but not replace a type system
claims.note: Industrial static analyzers deliberately trade soundness for coverage; this is their documented design position.

claims.text: Dynamic languages can run programs that are deliberately not statically type-safe, which helps when exploring or modifying large systems
claims.note: Running partially broken code aids exploration, but gradual typing and IDE tooling narrow the gap.

claims.text: Unit tests catch most type errors and can give guarantees beyond what static typing provides
claims.note: Tests check behaviour that types cannot express, but they are not exhaustive, so types and tests are complementary rather than one subsuming the other.

claims.text: Mainstream static type systems cannot express many useful constraints, such as a divisor being non-zero
claims.note: Refinement and dependent types can express such constraints but remain niche; mainstream systems cannot.

claims.text: Small increases in type system expressiveness cause disproportionately large increases in complexity
claims.note: Borne out by the history of Scala, Java generics and TypeScript's type-level programming, though it is a qualitative observation.

claims.text: Type systems themselves contain soundness bugs that are hard to fix without breaking existing programs
claims.note: Eiffel covariance, Java generics with arrays, and unsoundness found in Scala and TypeScript are documented cases.

claims.text: Automatic memory management saves a large share of programmer time and removes a class of bugs
claims.note: Memory-safety bugs are the majority of serious vulnerabilities in C and C++ codebases per Microsoft and Google data.

claims.text: Short-lived feature branches with pull requests preserve the benefits of trunk-based development as long as they merge within a day or so
claims.note: Branch lifetime, not branch existence, drives integration pain; this is the consensus position in continuous delivery literature.

claims.text: Teams on a shared trunk can scale headcount up or down without losing throughput or quality
claims.note: Google's monorepo shows it is possible with heavy tooling investment; Brooks's-law effects do not vanish because of a branching model.

claims.text: Beyond a couple of developers a build server is needed to catch commits that break the trunk
claims.note: CI servers are near-universal practice; the threshold is a rule of thumb.

claims.text: Tools that assign a monetary figure to technical debt produce made-up numbers
claims.note: SQALE-style remediation costs rest on arbitrary per-issue estimates with little validation; some correlate loosely with maintenance effort.

claims.text: Organizations often scale headcount to cope with the mess created by their own neglect rather than to add value
claims.note: Plausible but no data links hiring growth to failure demand.

claims.text: Unmanaged technical debt undermines security because code and dependencies nobody understands cannot be reasoned about
claims.note: Dependency unawareness is a documented supply-chain risk; the link to general debt is argued rather than measured.

claims.text: Focusing on one change inevitably leaves side-effect mess that must be cleaned up afterwards
claims.note: Lehman's increasing-complexity law; empirical decay studies support it, though the inevitability is a strong form.

claims.text: Code does not decay on its own; degradation comes from the changes made to it
claims.note: True of the code text; in practice environments and dependencies drift, so untouched code does stop working.

claims.text: Capping pull request size makes developers chain dependent branches instead of working in smaller steps
claims.note: Stacked PRs are a common response to size limits; whether that is worse than large PRs is unmeasured.

claims.text: Working together builds psychological safety better than anything else
claims.note: Collaboration correlates with safety, but the superlative is attributed to unnamed research.

claims.text: Pairing makes waste like slow builds visible and fixed because two people waiting will not tolerate what one accepts
claims.note: Plausible social mechanism reported by one team; no independent evidence.

claims.text: Per-change pull request gates break down under continuous delivery with many deployments a day
claims.note: More than 25,000 Google developers put about 20,000 changes a day through mandatory per-change review into one trunk, with median latency under 4 hours and developers confirming the process works well at scale; one highly tuned company, not a GitHub pull-request setup.

claims.text: Software complexity is whatever makes a system hard to understand and modify, and is judged by its readers rather than its writers
claims.note: Understandability proxies varied more between developers reading the same snippet than between snippets read by the same developer, and none of 121 code metrics captured it, supporting that difficulty is reader-dependent; the claim's definition of complexity itself is not tested.

claims.text: Defining errors out of existence at the interface removes whole classes of error handling
claims.note: Works for idempotent operations like unset; many errors reflect real external failures that cannot be defined away.

claims.text: Consistency across a codebase is worth more than any individual better idea that would break it
claims.note: Consistency aids comprehension in code-reading studies, but 'almost always' ignores cases where a convention is actively harmful.

claims.text: Productivity being hard to measure does not prevent sound judgments about large differences between people
claims.note: Epistemic framing rather than a testable claim.

claims.text: Relative-size estimation is more accurate than time estimates for complex or uncertain work
claims.note: Few studies exist; relative estimation improved accuracy in some contexts and worsened it in others, and the authors conclude relative predictions are generally not more accurate than absolute ones and bias estimates when tasks differ much in size.

claims.text: Group estimation sessions surface hidden complexity and build shared understanding of the work
claims.note: Groups of software professionals produced higher and more realistic estimates than their prior individual ones, qualitatively because they identified more activities, and planning poker gave a shared understanding of the work and risks; student groups, by contrast, became more optimistic.

claims.text: Velocity from completed points gives reliable forecasts of future throughput
claims.note: Extrapolating from measured early productivity is called 'a simple time prediction model based on highly local data' that few models beat, but reliability is not quantified and relative (point-based) estimation is elsewhere found no more accurate than absolute estimation.

claims.text: Time spent estimating is wasted and better spent building
claims.note: The review's authors reject the NoEstimates position that predictions are a waste as unrealistic, noting that extrapolating progress is itself a time prediction and that judgement-based predictions are on average fairly accurate (20-30% error).

claims.text: Abstract units shield teams from fixed-deadline pressure and reduce estimate padding
claims.note: Padding under pressure is documented, but stakeholders convert points to dates anyway, as the same source notes.

commonlyWrong.text: Estimation is a learnable skill: recording estimates and comparing them to outcomes calibrates future estimates
commonlyWrong.note: Independent studies of the Personal Software Process, which records estimates and analyses deviations from actuals, found no improvement in estimation accuracy, and a feedback-and-lessons-learned programme likewise produced none versus untrained controls.

commonlyWrong.text: Pairing's value cannot be proven scientifically because development output is too hard to measure, so teams must try it themselves
commonlyWrong.note: The review describes research on particular practices like pair programming as at an intermediate or even mature state, and cites an earlier review calling pair programming supported by a well-established research stream; the evidence may be mixed, but the authors treat it as a scientifically studiable question, not an unmeasurable one.

commonlyWrong.text: Per-change pull request gates break down under continuous delivery with many deployments a day
commonlyWrong.note: More than 25,000 Google developers put about 20,000 changes a day through mandatory per-change review into one trunk, with median latency under 4 hours and developers confirming the process works well at scale; one highly tuned company, not a GitHub pull-request setup.

commonlyWrong.text: Relative-size estimation is more accurate than time estimates for complex or uncertain work
commonlyWrong.note: Few studies exist; relative estimation improved accuracy in some contexts and worsened it in others, and the authors conclude relative predictions are generally not more accurate than absolute ones and bias estimates when tasks differ much in size.

commonlyWrong.text: Time spent estimating is wasted and better spent building
commonlyWrong.note: The review's authors reject the NoEstimates position that predictions are a waste as unrealistic, noting that extrapolating progress is itself a time prediction and that judgement-based predictions are on average fairly accurate (20-30% error).

claim.text: Reviewer defect-finding effectiveness drops sharply once a single review exceeds a few hundred lines
claim.note: The SmartBear Cisco field study found defect density per line falling past roughly 200-400 lines per review, though it is a single vendor-run industrial dataset rather than a controlled experiment.

priorRecord.note: The SmartBear Cisco field study found defect density per line falling past roughly 200-400 lines per review, though it is a single vendor-run industrial dataset rather than a controlled experiment.

evidenceRecord.note: Changes approved faster than 200 lines per hour ('hastily reviewed') are associated with more post-release defects in Qt 5.1.0, and only 10% of such changes are needed before a component is expected to have a defect; this is about review rate, not a fixed lines-per-review threshold.

claim.text: Sustained crunch lowers productivity and employee happiness
claim.note: Labour economics and reviews of overtime research show output per hour falls and errors rise after sustained weeks beyond roughly fifty hours, and burnout studies link crunch to attrition.

priorRecord.note: Labour economics and reviews of overtime research show output per hour falls and errors rise after sustained weeks beyond roughly fifty hours, and burnout studies link crunch to attrition.

evidenceRecord.note: 122 weekly observations on WWI munitions workers: output is proportional to hours below 49 h/week, rises at a decreasing rate above it and peaks near 63 h, so output per hour falls once weeks run long; happiness was not measured and the workers were not programmers.

claim.text: Long-lived branches delay integration and produce merge conflicts that grow with team size
claim.note: The mechanism is direct, and DORA research associates short-lived branches and trunk-based development with higher delivery performance.

priorRecord.note: The mechanism is direct, and DORA research associates short-lived branches and trunk-based development with higher delivery performance.

evidenceRecord.note: DORA observes that merging patches sooner avoids rebases and that short-lived branches and small patches make everyone more productive, but it does not measure merge conflicts or how they scale with team size.

claim.text: Running a CI server is not continuous integration if branches live for days or weeks
