thinEvidence.note: A design-perception claim with no agreed measure.

thinEvidence.text: Comments that restate code are noise and drift out of date because nothing checks them
thinEvidence.note: Studies find comment-code inconsistency common after change, but comprehension research also shows explanatory comments help readers, so the claim holds for restating comments not all comments.

thinEvidence.text: Crunch is a symptom of poor planning, especially failing to schedule testing and iteration time
thinEvidence.note: Postmortems and case studies link crunch to scope and schedule failures, but publisher deadlines, funding and studio culture also drive it, so planning is one cause among several.

thinEvidence.text: Debt is prudent when taken deliberately to ship sooner with small interest, and reckless when taken without understanding its cost
thinEvidence.note: Classification framework.

thinEvidence.text: Decomposing code into very small methods can go too far, producing shallow interfaces and entangled methods that are harder to read than one longer method
thinEvidence.note: Controlled studies find no comprehension gain from splitting code into very small methods, though none establishes where the optimum lies.

thinEvidence.text: Decomposing a monolith only works if it already has a reasonably modular design; tangled monoliths just produce a mess
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with migration case studies, though some decompositions of tangled code succeeded with heavy investment.

thinEvidence.text: Driving architecture from unit tests without an up-front domain model yields a procedural, bottom-up design that cannot be refactored out of.
thinEvidence.note: Design damage from test-driven isolation is reported in case studies and the DHH debate, but controlled studies of TDD's design effects are mixed and small.

thinEvidence.text: Dynamic languages can run programs that are deliberately not statically type-safe, which helps when exploring or modifying large systems
thinEvidence.note: Running partially broken code aids exploration, but gradual typing and IDE tooling narrow the gap.

thinEvidence.text: Early in a system's life little design is needed; design investment should start when feature speed begins to slow
thinEvidence.note: Fowler's design stamina hypothesis is a hypothesis; consistent with debt-payoff reasoning.

thinEvidence.text: Feature flags let unfinished work merge to trunk and decouple deployment from release
thinEvidence.note: A well-established mechanism used at scale by large web companies, with documented costs in flag management.

thinEvidence.text: Following clean-code structure rules can cost performance equivalent to a decade or more of hardware improvement
thinEvidence.note: Holds for the toy benchmark; in typical applications I/O, allocation and network dominate so the end-to-end cost is far smaller.

thinEvidence.text: Fusing data layout with the operation in table-driven, data-oriented code can be an order of magnitude faster than encapsulated class hierarchies
thinEvidence.note: Well-known data-oriented design result for compute-bound loops; most application code is not compute-bound.

thinEvidence.text: AI-generated code volume outruns fixed human review capacity, making code review the bottleneck on shipping software
thinEvidence.note: One large telemetry study reports code output rising far faster than shipped software after agent adoption, but attributing the gap to review is the authors' inference and other bottlenecks (testing, deployment, product decisions) are not separated out.

thinEvidence.text: Hiring super-programmers is a poor route to team productivity compared with improving the working environment.
thinEvidence.note: Follows from the variance finding, but environmental interventions have not been compared head-to-head with hiring in controlled studies.

thinEvidence.text: Hitting an estimate has no value if the software built is the wrong thing.
thinEvidence.note: A framing about what counts as success rather than a measurable claim.

thinEvidence.text: Pairs sustain focus better than individuals working alone.
thinEvidence.note: Reported in pair-programming studies as 'pair pressure', mostly self-reported.

thinEvidence.text: A rewrite team is unlikely to do better because it lacks the original team's experience and repeats old mistakes.
thinEvidence.note: Second-system effects are documented, but a rewrite with clearer requirements can succeed.

thinEvidence.text: The right mix of unit and higher-level tests depends on where a system's complexity lives, not on fixed pyramid ratios.
thinEvidence.note: Reasonable and consistent with practice, but no study compares test-mix strategies against outcomes.

thinEvidence.text: Rotating the driver every few minutes keeps every team member engaged
thinEvidence.note: Engagement is self-reported; no comparative data.

thinEvidence.text: Rote, repetitive code is a design smell, and pairing helps find the missing abstraction
thinEvidence.note: Plausible; no evidence.

thinEvidence.text: Services that always change together should be merged or re-sliced
thinEvidence.note: A design heuristic; co-change analysis can detect the pattern but whether merging is right is a judgment.

thinEvidence.text: Skipping architecture review in a project's first weeks locks in decisions that take years to undo
thinEvidence.note: Early structural decisions are the costliest to reverse, though the exponential defect-cost curve behind this is overstated.

thinEvidence.text: Very small changes can be worse than mid-sized ones because their implications are hidden and they are reverted more often
thinEvidence.note: One vendor dataset shows higher revert rates under ten lines, plausibly from config changes; the pattern has not been replicated.

thinEvidence.text: TDD biases design toward extra abstraction and indirection, which harms clarity unless the designer pushes back.
thinEvidence.note: Test-induced indirection is widely reported in practice and in the DHH debate, but controlled studies of TDD on design quality show small mixed effects.

thinEvidence.text: Teams that stop reading agent-written code accumulate hidden defects that later force large rewrites
thinEvidence.note: Supported by a public retraction and by audits of agent-ported code finding unusual numbers of unsafe constructs, but the evidence is anecdotal with no controlled comparison.

thinEvidence.text: Testing advocacy has become a dogma that shames developers who do not follow it
thinEvidence.note: A claim about community culture and tone, not a measurable effect.

thinEvidence.text: Tests serve as precise, unambiguous low-level documentation of the system
thinEvidence.note: Tests document behaviour but are hard to navigate as documentation; evidence is practitioner opinion.

thinEvidence.text: Writing a test per method and mocking every dependency couples tests to implementation so refactoring breaks them
thinEvidence.note: Over-specified interaction tests are a documented cause of fragile suites in both practitioner literature and studies of test co-evolution.

thinEvidence.text: Adding public interfaces around modules without untangling the dependency graph just adds indirection and makes code harder to change
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with coupling research and Parnas-style modularity theory, but the evidence here is one organization's experience report.

thinEvidence.text: Adopting microservices without changing the organisation yields the costs without the benefits
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with Conway's law research and practitioner reports, but it is an expert judgment rather than a measured outcome.

thinEvidence.text: After-the-fact code review is weaker than pairing because reviewers skim, defer to the author and resist rework already invested
thinEvidence.note: Microsoft studies show reviews catch fewer defects than expected, but head-to-head comparisons with pairing are lacking.

thinEvidence.text: Agile has been turned from an adjective into a product sold through certification, training and consultancy, losing the original values
thinEvidence.note: A historical and framing claim about an industry, not a measurable outcome.

thinEvidence.text: Almost any large change can be decomposed into a series of small ones by an author who practises it
thinEvidence.note: Stacking and vertical slicing work for most feature work, but generated code, large migrations and some refactors resist splitting.

thinEvidence.text: Apparent standout productivity can reflect tenure, project selection, information hoarding or credit-taking rather than skill
thinEvidence.note: Plausible confounders; no study separates them from genuine skill differences.

thinEvidence.text: Assigning people to review code full time to absorb more volume burns reviewers out
thinEvidence.note: Review fatigue and the tedium of full-time review are widely reported by practitioners, but there is no measured burnout study specific to this arrangement.

thinEvidence.text: Automated code reviewers are fooled by confidently framed malicious changes far more often than human reviewers
thinEvidence.note: Prompt injection against LLM reviewers is a documented weakness and vendors warn about it themselves, but the specific human-versus-agent comparison comes from a single study.

thinEvidence.text: Automated refactoring tools have existed for decades yet legacy code persists, so the obstacle is mindset not tooling
thinEvidence.note: Tool-usage studies show refactoring tools are underused, which supports the mindset explanation.

thinEvidence.text: An automated test is an investment that permanently prevents the class of problem it checks.
thinEvidence.note: Regression tests do prevent recurrence, but suites also incur maintenance and decay, which the claim ignores.

thinEvidence.text: Automated tests give little feedback on whether a feature serves users or whether the codebase is healthy.
thinEvidence.note: Tests check specified behaviour; user value and design health need other feedback, though some tests target design.

thinEvidence.text: Automating everything except creative judgment makes releases repeatable and reliable because humans are not.
thinEvidence.note: Deployment automation correlates with lower change failure in DORA data; human error in manual deployments is well documented.

thinEvidence.text: Automating scripted QA checks lets teams get release answers in hours instead of weeks.
thinEvidence.note: Test automation shortens feedback cycles in DORA and industrial reports; the gain depends on suite quality.

thinEvidence.text: Avoiding repeated code does not conflict with writing fast code
thinEvidence.note: Reasonable in general; some performance work deliberately duplicates code paths for specialisation.

thinEvidence.text: Best practices are inherited from what the most successful programmers do, which cannot distinguish good techniques from bad ones they succeed despite
thinEvidence.note: The logic holds and practice adoption is visibly driven by prominent advocates, but how much of practice folklore actually originates this way is not measured.

thinEvidence.text: Beyond a couple of developers a build server is needed to catch commits that break the trunk
thinEvidence.note: CI servers are near-universal practice; the threshold is a rule of thumb.

thinEvidence.text: Caffeine tolerance builds within days, so it cannot offset extended overtime.
thinEvidence.note: Tolerance to caffeine's alerting effects develops within days to a week in most studies, though partial benefits persist for some.

thinEvidence.text: Being on call for production teaches developers which tests and feedback loops they are missing.
thinEvidence.note: A reasonable mechanism consistent with DevOps practice; not measured.

thinEvidence.text: Capping pull request size makes developers chain dependent branches instead of working in smaller steps
thinEvidence.note: Stacked PRs are a common response to size limits; whether that is worse than large PRs is unmeasured.

thinEvidence.text: A change passing its test suite is a weak proxy for whether a maintainer would actually merge it
thinEvidence.note: Tests only cover specified behaviour and cannot see maintainability, scope or hidden coupling; the METR maintainer study cited here supports this, though it is one study on agent-written PRs.

thinEvidence.text: Checklists catch omission defects that unstructured review tends to miss
thinEvidence.note: Checklist-based reading experiments show modest gains over ad hoc reading; 'most effective' is overstated.

thinEvidence.text: Choosing the right algorithm improves efficiency by many orders of magnitude while cycle-level tuning gives about one
thinEvidence.note: Asymptotic improvements dominate constant-factor ones on large inputs, though for fixed-size hot loops constant factors are all that remain.

thinEvidence.text: Choosing which features to release after integration testing means shipping a combination that was never tested
thinEvidence.note: Logically sound; the size of the risk depends on how coupled the features are.

thinEvidence.text: The claim that defect fix cost rises exponentially by lifecycle phase has no verifiable measurement behind it
thinEvidence.note: Boehm's original data exists but is thinner than the derived charts; modern iterative projects show much flatter curves.

thinEvidence.text: Class-level unit tests are hard to trace to business value.
thinEvidence.note: A judgment about traceability rather than a measurable claim.

thinEvidence.text: Clean Code teaching gives performance almost no attention, so its audience learns to ignore it
thinEvidence.note: The author conceded the point about his own lecture series; whether audiences actually absorb a disregard for performance is not measured.

thinEvidence.text: Clustering meetings at the end of the day preserves uninterrupted maker time
thinEvidence.note: Follows from interruption cost; no outcome data.

thinEvidence.text: Code does not decay on its own; degradation comes from the changes made to it
thinEvidence.note: True of the code text; in practice environments and dependencies drift, so untouched code does stop working.

thinEvidence.text: Coding conventions spread by repetition rather than understanding, producing cargo-cult practices
thinEvidence.note: A sociological framing about how practices propagate.

thinEvidence.text: AI coding tools reproduce a codebase's existing anti-patterns unless a new pattern is established first
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with how code models condition on context; measured mainly in practitioner reports.

thinEvidence.text: Combining unit and integration tests catches more than integration tests alone
thinEvidence.note: Different test levels find different fault classes, but no study quantifies the marginal catch of adding unit tests to a good integration suite.

thinEvidence.text: The cone of uncertainty in estimation has no empirical basis
thinEvidence.note: Boehm presented it as a notional diagram; later project data did not show estimates narrowing as the cone predicts.

thinEvidence.text: Confidence from programmer-written tests led many teams to drop QA and ship lower quality.
thinEvidence.note: Anecdotal; some companies did cut QA, but no study links this to measured quality loss.

thinEvidence.text: Consistency across a codebase is worth more than any individual better idea that would break it
thinEvidence.note: Consistency aids comprehension in code-reading studies, but 'almost always' ignores cases where a convention is actively harmful.

thinEvidence.text: Creating services by which team is free rather than by domain seams produces fragmented systems
thinEvidence.note: Conway's-law reasoning and anecdote; no measured outcome data.

thinEvidence.text: Customer-readable acceptance test suites are rarely read by customers and carry a heavy maintenance burden
thinEvidence.note: Practitioner consensus including the Fit author's own retraction supports this, though some teams report value from Gherkin-style specs; no controlled study exists.

thinEvidence.text: The debt metaphor helps explain design problems to non-technical stakeholders
thinEvidence.note: Communication framing.

thinEvidence.text: Defining errors out of existence at the interface removes whole classes of error handling
thinEvidence.note: Works for idempotent operations like unset; many errors reflect real external failures that cannot be defined away.

thinEvidence.text: Dependency inversion via polymorphism protects high-level policy from recompilation and redeployment when low-level details change
thinEvidence.note: The mechanism is real, but link-time binding through opaque pointers gives the same isolation, so the benefit specific to runtime polymorphism is mainly plugins and frameworks.

thinEvidence.text: Design by contract covers the whole input range of a method, giving broader assurance than sampled unit tests.
thinEvidence.note: Contracts specify behaviour over all inputs but are only enforced on executed inputs unless statically verified, so coverage gains depend on tooling.

thinEvidence.text: Desirable test properties trade off; making tests more predictive of production makes them slower
thinEvidence.note: Integration and end-to-end tests are consistently slower than unit tests while catching more realistic failures; the test-pyramid literature rests on this.

thinEvidence.text: Developer-time savings claimed from ignoring performance are erased by later ground-up performance rewrites
thinEvidence.note: Several large companies have published performance-driven rewrites, but the examples are survivors whose slow first version reached market, so the net accounting is unknown.

thinEvidence.text: Developers do not care about DORA metrics, only about merging their code quickly
thinEvidence.note: A generalisation about motivation that varies by team.

thinEvidence.text: Developers who deploy their own work to production are happier because they see its impact
thinEvidence.note: DORA surveys associate continuous delivery with lower burnout and higher job satisfaction, but causation is not isolated and this is one team's impression.

thinEvidence.text: DORA metrics are retrospective and cannot be acted on until after code has shipped
thinEvidence.note: They are lagging indicators by construction, though teams routinely act on their trends, so the practical limitation is smaller than framed.

thinEvidence.text: Dynamic languages became popular because they gave fast feedback and concise syntax for early web work, not because dynamic typing is inherently better.
thinEvidence.note: A plausible historical account consistent with language-adoption timelines, but causal attribution from history is not testable.

thinEvidence.text: Easy-to-repeat claims act as curiosity stoppers that prevent investigating what actually makes projects succeed
thinEvidence.note: A framing claim about how folklore affects inquiry.

thinEvidence.text: Editors render comments in muted colors, which trains developers to ignore and neglect them.
thinEvidence.note: Syntax highlighting conventions do de-emphasize comments; whether that causes neglect is untested.

thinEvidence.text: Emergency changes made under stress usually skip testing, which is when testing is most needed.
thinEvidence.note: Skipped testing in emergency changes is widely reported in incident reviews but not quantified here.

thinEvidence.text: Encoding a dynamically typed program in a static type system bloats it with explicit checks the runtime would do implicitly
thinEvidence.note: True for naive sum-type encodings; gradual and inferred systems reduce but do not eliminate the annotation burden.

thinEvidence.text: End-to-end browser tests are brittle but the fastest way to get coverage from zero on a legacy system
thinEvidence.note: Matches the test-pyramid rationale; brittleness of UI tests is well documented.

thinEvidence.text: Ephemeral per-branch environments remove the bottleneck of shared test environments
thinEvidence.note: The queueing mechanism is sound and widely reported, but evidence is practitioner case studies and the environments bring their own cost and data-seeding work.

thinEvidence.text: Even excellent teams accumulate inadvertent debt because the right design is only learned by building the system
thinEvidence.note: Matches design-emergence research and practitioner consensus; not experimentally tested.

thinEvidence.text: Every change that adds or alters logic should ship with its tests in the same change
thinEvidence.note: Widely adopted policy, but no study compares co-committed tests against tests landed separately.

thinEvidence.text: Experience, lines of code written and degrees held did not predict programmer productivity.
thinEvidence.note: This null result holds in the PSP dataset, but other studies find modest effects of relevant experience, so it is not settled.

thinEvidence.text: Explicit module ownership makes whole-codebase chores like framework upgrades easier to distribute
thinEvidence.note: Ownership clarity is linked to lower defect rates in Microsoft's organizational-metrics studies, but the upgrade claim is a single report.

thinEvidence.text: Extensive automated pre-submit checks catch most breaking changes before they are merged
thinEvidence.note: Pre-submit CI catches many regressions, but the share depends on test coverage; the figure is a personal estimate.

thinEvidence.text: Extracting one slice with divergent performance needs as a separate service captures most of the scaling benefit without distributing the whole system
thinEvidence.note: Targeted extraction is a standard migration pattern and matches Shopify's and others' reports, but 'most of the benefit' is not quantified.

thinEvidence.text: Faster, more responsive software measurably increases user engagement and revenue
thinEvidence.note: Published latency experiments at Amazon, Google and others consistently show engagement and conversion dropping with added delay, though 'conclusive' overstates how far the effect generalises to internal tools.

thinEvidence.text: Feature flags carry an ongoing removal cost that teams must schedule and pay back
thinEvidence.note: Stale-flag debt is well documented and large companies have built tooling specifically to remove dead flags.

thinEvidence.text: Feature toggles are a hack and a source of errors that proper branch-per-feature avoids
thinEvidence.note: Toggle debt and misconfiguration incidents are real, but branches trade them for merge risk; no comparison exists.

thinEvidence.text: Focusing on one change inevitably leaves side-effect mess that must be cleaned up afterwards
thinEvidence.note: Lehman's increasing-complexity law; empirical decay studies support it, though the inevitability is a strong form.

thinEvidence.text: A full day of rest after a missed night of sleep does not restore performance to baseline.
thinEvidence.note: Shift-work recovery studies support incomplete recovery after one night; the size depends on the deficit.

thinEvidence.text: Function-length rules such as fit on one screen came from historical terminal sizes, not evidence
thinEvidence.note: Historical framing.

thinEvidence.text: Game features need more iteration than business software because feel and fun cannot be specified on paper
thinEvidence.note: A judgment about the nature of the work rather than a measurable claim.

thinEvidence.text: Generic repository abstractions over an ORM lead to N+1 queries and joining in application memory
thinEvidence.note: A commonly documented .NET anti-pattern; the problem is the abstraction's inflexibility rather than inevitability.

thinEvidence.text: Getting a test to green with quick dirty code and then refactoring is faster than engineering the design up front
thinEvidence.note: Kent Beck's original claim, consistent with cognitive-load arguments against solving and designing at once, but not directly measured.

thinEvidence.text: Giving accurate timelines builds trust and is required to advance beyond senior engineering roles
thinEvidence.note: Career advice.

thinEvidence.text: Giving requirements without having the engineer explain them back leads to them being silently ignored
thinEvidence.note: Read-back is standard in safety-critical communication; software evidence is anecdotal.

thinEvidence.text: A good design is one that is easier to change than a bad design, and every design principle follows from that
thinEvidence.note: A definition and design heuristic rather than a prediction.

thinEvidence.text: Gradual typing requires a more complex type system and keeps dynamic runtime overhead, so it is not the best of both worlds.
thinEvidence.note: Type-system complexity in TypeScript and Sorbet supports this, though gradual typing's migration benefit is real.

thinEvidence.text: GUI-driven integration tests cannot reach a large fraction of code such as error handling and edge cases
thinEvidence.note: Coverage from end-to-end tests is typically well below unit-level coverage; the 'bit more than half' figure is a guess.

thinEvidence.text: Having the whole team at one keyboard eliminates waiting for answers to blocking questions
thinEvidence.note: The mechanism follows directly from having all needed skills present, and mob case studies report it, but there is no controlled comparison and it depends on the product owner being present too.

thinEvidence.text: Headlines about big companies abandoning microservices usually describe one team consolidating a few components
thinEvidence.note: The Prime Video post concerned one team's service; Amazon overall remained service-based.

thinEvidence.text: Higher-level behavioural tests make mutation testing more practical than many fine-grained unit tests
thinEvidence.note: A practitioner hunch; fewer larger tests may run slower per mutant, so the net effect on runtime is unclear.

thinEvidence.text: The human role in code review is shifting from reading diffs to designing and tuning the systems that inspect code
thinEvidence.note: A forecast about how roles will evolve rather than a claim that can be checked against evidence.

thinEvidence.text: Imposing uniform coding conventions adds learning and compliance friction without making hard design problems easier
thinEvidence.note: Rules have a cost, but consistency also has measured comprehension benefits, so the net effect depends on the rule.

thinEvidence.text: The impossibility of exhaustively testing a program's state space applies to integration tests as much as unit tests
thinEvidence.note: Both are samples, but a system-level test exercises many units per case, so the argument cuts differently per test.

thinEvidence.text: Interactive and visual behaviour such as GUIs and game feel cannot practically be test-driven because the correct answer is not known up front
thinEvidence.note: Both debaters and the game industry agree; snapshot and replay testing cover regressions but not the initial judgement of correctness.

thinEvidence.text: Juniors who always pair can lose confidence and miss learning to solve problems alone
thinEvidence.note: Plausible and reported, though novice studies mostly show pairing helps juniors.

thinEvidence.text: Keeping a branch per feature lets a finished feature be pulled before release, which trunk-based development cannot do
thinEvidence.note: True without toggles; feature flags give trunk-based teams the same ability at some complexity cost.

thinEvidence.text: Keeping code clean enough to keep development fast is worth more than the cost of building a trustworthy test suite
thinEvidence.note: A cost-benefit judgment with no agreed way to measure either side.

thinEvidence.text: Large functions are classes in disguise; extracting until stuck reveals hidden classes
thinEvidence.note: Extract Class from shared locals is a standard refactoring; 'every' overstates.

thinEvidence.text: Large-scale architecture refactors stay in an incomplete intermediate state far longer than planned
thinEvidence.note: Widely reported across migration case studies, but it is experience-based rather than measured.

thinEvidence.text: Letting workers choose their own hours improves satisfaction, health and productivity.
thinEvidence.note: Schedule control shows consistent positive associations in occupational health research, but effects are moderate and mostly observational.

thinEvidence.text: Lightweight tool-assisted review finds as many defects as formal inspection in a fraction of the time
thinEvidence.note: Vendor data; independent studies (Bacchelli and Bird) find modern lightweight review catches fewer defects than expected, with most value in knowledge transfer.

thinEvidence.text: Logging without stated requirements grows until it dominates the codebase
thinEvidence.note: Anecdotal from client codebases; no measurement of logging proportion across projects.

thinEvidence.text: Making expert advocates argue opposing positions publicly is a partial substitute for missing research
thinEvidence.note: A preference about discourse rather than a prediction that could be checked.

thinEvidence.text: Making a failing test pass gives a small reward that makes test-first more enjoyable than writing tests afterwards
thinEvidence.note: A claim about enjoyment and motivation that varies by person.

thinEvidence.text: Managers and makers run on different schedules, and conflict arises when hourly manager slots are imposed on makers
thinEvidence.note: Framing.

thinEvidence.text: Many small services make it easy for knowledge to silo so only one person understands each part
thinEvidence.note: Service ownership does concentrate knowledge by design; whether that is worse than monolith hotspots has not been measured.

thinEvidence.text: Many teams that adopted microservices are retreating to monoliths
thinEvidence.note: There are prominent consolidation stories (Amazon Prime Video, Segment) but no survey establishes a net trend.

thinEvidence.text: Maturity models go out of date too quickly to guide technology transformations.
thinEvidence.note: An argument about how to frame a transformation, not a measured outcome.

thinEvidence.text: Merge tools cannot detect functional conflicts between independently developed features; only integrating and testing can
thinEvidence.note: Semantic conflicts are invisible to textual merge; this is the standard rationale for CI.

thinEvidence.text: 'Micro' should mean replaceable, not few lines of code
thinEvidence.note: Definitional.

thinEvidence.text: In a mob the group coaches a less-skilled driver on the spot, raising everyone's skills
thinEvidence.note: Case reports from Hunter Industries and others are positive; no controlled studies.

thinEvidence.text: Mob programming finishes stories in hours that took individuals working separately weeks
thinEvidence.note: Self-reported from one team with the speaker himself saying the card comparison is not proof; no independent measurement of mob throughput exists.

thinEvidence.text: Modules can only be reasoned about or tested in isolation when the dependency graph between them is sparse and acyclic
thinEvidence.note: Follows from how dependencies propagate change; cyclic dependency metrics correlate with defect proneness in several empirical studies.

thinEvidence.text: Monoliths without enforced boundaries become so coupled that small changes have unexpected effects and newcomers need enormous context
thinEvidence.note: Coupling-defect and comprehension research supports it; Shopify's developer survey is a single case.

thinEvidence.text: Most of a long backlog is wasted because items far down will change before they are reached.
thinEvidence.note: Requirements volatility is well documented; the claim that distant items are nearly worthless is plausible but unmeasured.

thinEvidence.text: Most software developers, including game developers, work roughly normal hours with only occasional overtime
thinEvidence.note: Industry surveys such as IGDA's find crunch still common in games with roughly half of respondents reporting it, so the picture is mixed; the video's own survey is small and self-selected.

thinEvidence.text: Much delivered functionality is rarely or never used, so working through a prioritised backlog wastes effort compared with selecting high-impact items
thinEvidence.note: The widely cited 64% figure comes from a small Standish sample; feature usage is skewed but the magnitude is unknown.

thinEvidence.text: Much developer overtime is self-imposed from passion rather than mandated by employers
thinEvidence.note: Surveys find both self-driven and management-driven crunch, and normative pressure makes voluntary overtime hard to separate from expected overtime.

thinEvidence.text: Mutation testing is too slow to run routinely without parallelisation or incremental selection
thinEvidence.note: Runtime is the documented adoption barrier; Google's deployment runs mutation analysis only on changed lines for this reason.

thinEvidence.text: Nearly every mainstream language that emerged after the 2000s is statically typed.
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with RedMonk and similar rankings, with a few exceptions.

thinEvidence.text: Never trust a test you have not seen fail
thinEvidence.note: Mutation testing routinely finds tests that cannot fail; seeing the red state is the standard guard.

thinEvidence.text: Non-blocking type errors keep the fast feedback of static types without preventing you from running code or tests.
thinEvidence.note: TypeScript's emit-on-error demonstrates feasibility; the productivity claim is anecdotal.

thinEvidence.text: Observed benefits of small PRs are partly selection: teams already practising trunk-based development make smaller PRs
thinEvidence.note: The author flags the confound; no study randomises PR size, so some of the correlation is team maturity.

thinEvidence.text: Organising code by business domain rather than technical layer makes code and its owners easier to find
thinEvidence.note: Package-by-feature is widely recommended; the evidence is practitioner experience.

thinEvidence.text: Organizations often scale headcount to cope with the mess created by their own neglect rather than to add value
thinEvidence.note: Plausible but no data links hiring growth to failure demand.

thinEvidence.text: Pairing limits team work in progress, which improves flow
thinEvidence.note: WIP limits improve flow in Kanban studies; attributing that to pairing is inference.

thinEvidence.text: Pairing makes waste like slow builds visible and fixed because two people waiting will not tolerate what one accepts
thinEvidence.note: Plausible social mechanism reported by one team; no independent evidence.

thinEvidence.text: Pairing pays off on novel, hard work and wastes effort on routine or repetitive tasks
thinEvidence.note: Meta-analysis finds pairing's benefit concentrated on complex tasks, consistent with this.

thinEvidence.text: The paper that introduced the waterfall diagram warned that the approach was risky and invited failure.
thinEvidence.note: Royce's 1970 paper does say the simple sequential model is risky and invites failure and recommends iteration.

thinEvidence.text: Performance must be designed in from the start because hotspot optimisation cannot fix serial dependency chains and poor data layout later
thinEvidence.note: Architectural choices like synchronous call chains are expensive to undo, but profiling-driven fixes resolve many real slowdowns without redesign.

thinEvidence.text: The performance penalty of class-hierarchy designs grows as the problem gets more complex
thinEvidence.note: Adding a second virtual call widened the gap here, but this is one extra property on a toy problem.

thinEvidence.text: Performance problems concentrate in a small part of a system, so targeted optimization beats a full rewrite.
thinEvidence.note: Hotspot concentration is a well-established profiling finding; the exact ratio varies.

thinEvidence.text: A performance trade-off only counts as a trade-off if the cost was measured; otherwise it is an excuse
thinEvidence.note: This is a framing about what deserves the word trade-off rather than a testable prediction.

thinEvidence.text: Polymorphism makes adding new types easy while switch statements make adding new operations easy; neither is a free win
thinEvidence.note: This is the well-known expression problem; the two designs are mirror images for the two kinds of extension.

thinEvidence.text: Power dynamics such as seniority or gender distort pairing when one person dominates the keyboard or dismisses suggestions
thinEvidence.note: Qualitative studies document the dynamic; its effect on outcomes is unmeasured.

thinEvidence.text: The 'premature optimisation' quote is misapplied as licence to ignore performance during design when it only warned against early micro-level hand tuning
thinEvidence.note: The full Knuth passage explicitly says not to pass up the critical few percent and concerns small-scale efficiencies, not architecture.

thinEvidence.text: Prioritising refactoring by hotspots, where change frequency meets low code health, targets the debt with the highest interest
thinEvidence.note: Change-frequency weighting is a sensible proxy supported by defect-prediction research, but comparative outcome data is limited to vendor case studies.

thinEvidence.text: Process boundaries enforce modularity that in-process modules fail to because languages let developers violate them
thinEvidence.note: Architecture erosion studies confirm in-process modules decay, but distributed monoliths show process boundaries get violated too via shared databases and chatty coupling.

thinEvidence.text: Productivity being hard to measure does not prevent sound judgments about large differences between people
thinEvidence.note: Epistemic framing rather than a testable claim.

thinEvidence.text: Programs are rarely inherently I/O bound; chatty serial chains of dependent requests make them look I/O bound
thinEvidence.note: Waterfall request chains are a well-documented cause of slow web apps, but large-data workloads genuinely are bounded by storage and network even when well structured.

thinEvidence.text: Pull requests spend about half their lifetime idle waiting for someone
thinEvidence.note: A vendor dataset with a product to sell, though independent studies at Google and Microsoft also find review wait time dominates review cycle time.

thinEvidence.text: Reaching the top few percent in most activities mainly requires correcting basic, observable mistakes rather than talent
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with deliberate-practice findings, but the game evidence is observational and self-selected.

thinEvidence.text: The readability gains credited to class hierarchies come from cleaning up messy code, which well-named procedural code achieves equally well
thinEvidence.note: Comprehension experiments find naming and structure matter more than paradigm, but no study compares a tidy procedural version against a hierarchy on the same task.

thinEvidence.text: Refactor a problem on its own terms before migrating it to a different paradigm
thinEvidence.note: Methodological preference.

thinEvidence.text: In refactoring-oriented development most commits reposition code so that the final feature addition is a trivial change
thinEvidence.note: Describes a workflow; the ratio is one practitioner's anecdote.

thinEvidence.text: Refactoring in small behaviour-preserving steps with tests or compiler checks at each step avoids the big-bang breakage trap
thinEvidence.note: Core of Fowler's refactoring method; supported by practitioner evidence more than experiments.

thinEvidence.text: The refactoring step needs no new tests because behaviour is unchanged and already covered
thinEvidence.note: Practice advice that follows from the definition of refactoring; whether existing tests actually cover the behaviour is case by case.

thinEvidence.text: Refactorings should be in separate changes from feature work and bug fixes so reviewers can understand each
thinEvidence.note: Tangled changes are shown to confuse both reviewers and defect analysis, though no study measures the review-quality gain directly.

thinEvidence.text: Replacing guesswork with measured experiments is what makes software development an engineering discipline.
thinEvidence.note: A philosophy of practice rather than a measurable claim.

thinEvidence.text: Reusing an old feature flag can switch on dormant code paths with catastrophic results
thinEvidence.note: The Knight Capital incident is documented in the SEC order as a repurposed flag plus an incomplete deployment, and flag hygiene guidance exists because of such cases.

thinEvidence.text: An AI reviewer can take an automated first pass at a pull request before a human reviews it.
thinEvidence.note: AI review tools do produce first-pass comments; how much of the human review they replace is not independently measured.

thinEvidence.text: Reviewer effectiveness falls off after about an hour of continuous review
thinEvidence.note: Vigilance decrement is well established in general, but direct evidence for code review durations is thin and vendor-sourced.

thinEvidence.text: Reviewing code synchronously at commit time rather than asynchronously reduces merge delay and conflicts
thinEvidence.note: The delay-to-conflict link is well supported; whether synchronous review is practical at scale is less clear.

thinEvidence.text: A rewrite is viable when the codebase is small, the product is not the main revenue source and there is a compelling business case
thinEvidence.note: Derived from a handful of personal cases; plausible conditions with no broader data.

thinEvidence.text: Running several independent automated review passes and keeping only agreed findings reduces false positives and improves review quality
thinEvidence.note: Ensemble and self-consistency effects are well documented for language models, but the size of the review-quality gain rests on one academic paper and vendor reports.

thinEvidence.text: Runtime assertions complement but cannot replace unit tests because an assertion failure is still a production failure
thinEvidence.note: Assertions do catch what tests missed but after shipping; the two find overlapping faults at different costs.

thinEvidence.text: Scaled agile frameworks appeal to large organisations because they look complex, not because they are shown to work
thinEvidence.note: No controlled evidence either way on SAFe-style frameworks; adopter surveys are mixed and self-reported.

thinEvidence.text: Scope growth during a project is mostly value discovered while building, and following the original plan discards it
thinEvidence.note: Requirements do emerge during development, but scope creep also includes gold-plating and unmanaged change, so treating all of it as value is optimistic.

thinEvidence.text: Serverless lets small teams ship without managing infrastructure and often within free tiers
thinEvidence.note: True for low, bursty traffic; costs and limits bite at sustained load, as the same video's Prime Video case shows.

thinEvidence.text: Service boundaries must be repartitioned continually as the business changes, so owning microservices is never finished
thinEvidence.note: Domain drift is real; whether it demands service repartitioning rather than internal change depends on granularity.

thinEvidence.text: Short certification courses produce practitioners who follow prescribed steps without understanding why
thinEvidence.note: Plausible and consistent with cargo-cult reports, but no study links certification length to team outcomes.

thinEvidence.text: Short cycle times force small teams, automation and fewer handoffs, so continuous delivery drives out lean and agile practices as a side effect.
thinEvidence.note: Logically coherent and consistent with DORA's capability model, but the causal direction is asserted, not measured.

thinEvidence.text: Short daily retrospectives keep improvement on track better than infrequent longer ones
thinEvidence.note: Plausible by analogy to frequent feedback loops but no study compares retrospective cadence.

thinEvidence.text: Shortening sprints too far increases estimation uncertainty because each sprint samples less work.
thinEvidence.note: Statistically sound for sprint-level forecasting, but no study pins down where the diminishing returns begin.

thinEvidence.text: Simple tests of error-handling paths could prevent most catastrophic failures in distributed systems
thinEvidence.note: A study of production outages in major distributed systems found most catastrophic failures stemmed from trivially testable error-handling bugs.

thinEvidence.text: No single architecture suits every scale, so architecture should be revisited with each order of magnitude of growth
thinEvidence.note: Heuristic.

thinEvidence.text: A single-process design suits long-running compute jobs and predictable traffic better than serverless functions
thinEvidence.note: Lambda pricing and duration limits make this true for sustained workloads; Cockcroft's advice is widely echoed.

thinEvidence.text: Sleep, stress and hours worked affect output more than any technical practice.
thinEvidence.note: Fatigue effects are large and robust, but no study directly compares them against technical practices on the same scale.

thinEvidence.text: Slowing down to investigate a problem before coding reduces later cleanup
thinEvidence.note: Upfront understanding reduces rework in design studies, though the optimal amount varies and this is an archetype, not data.

thinEvidence.text: Small increases in type system expressiveness cause disproportionately large increases in complexity
thinEvidence.note: Borne out by the history of Scala, Java generics and TypeScript's type-level programming, though it is a qualitative observation.

thinEvidence.text: A small team can maintain a large product across many platforms from a single integrated codebase
thinEvidence.note: Basecamp is a real existence proof, but a single company's experience does not show other approaches would have failed.

thinEvidence.text: Smaller companies tend to have somewhat more overtime than larger ones
thinEvidence.note: Based on a small informal survey; broader data on company size and hours in software is inconsistent.

thinEvidence.text: Static analysis is unsound and incomplete, so it can augment but not replace a type system
thinEvidence.note: Industrial static analyzers deliberately trade soundness for coverage; this is their documented design position.

thinEvidence.text: Static dependency analysis gives faster and more actionable boundary enforcement than tracing runtime calls
thinEvidence.note: Static reference analysis is cheap and deterministic; dynamic tracing depends on test coverage and is noisy, though it catches reflective calls static analysis misses.

thinEvidence.text: Static typing forces implementing an entire interface up front even when only part of it is used.
thinEvidence.note: True of Java-style nominal interfaces; languages with structural typing or default methods avoid much of this cost.

thinEvidence.text: Story-point estimation and sprint commitment are alternative ways to fill an iteration, not complements
thinEvidence.note: A definitional stance on process design.

thinEvidence.text: Story-point velocity is only stable while the team is stable; adding or removing people changes it
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with Brooks's law and observed velocity volatility after staffing changes, though mostly practitioner data.

thinEvidence.text: Story points began as renamed ideal days, meant only to decide how much work fits an iteration
thinEvidence.note: Historical account from a participant.

thinEvidence.text: Story points forecast delivery only on average across several iterations, never for a single sprint
thinEvidence.note: Aggregate forecasting improves with history; per-sprint accuracy is poor in most reported data.

thinEvidence.text: Strict TDD, which forbids production code without a failing test, is incompatible with trading off coverage by criticality.
thinEvidence.note: A logical argument about methodology consistency rather than a measurable outcome.

thinEvidence.text: Sustained mob programming requires members to treat each other with kindness, consideration and respect
thinEvidence.note: A team norm whose necessity cannot be separated from the practice in available evidence.

thinEvidence.text: Switch-based code is easier to optimise later than a class hierarchy because all cases are visible in one place
thinEvidence.note: Merging cases into branch-free or vectorised code is standard practice and needs the cases in one place, but this is a specialist optimisation path rather than a general maintenance cost.

thinEvidence.text: Taking on small third-party dependencies for trivial functions adds fragility out of proportion to the code saved
thinEvidence.note: The left-pad incident and subsequent supply-chain research show deep transitive dependency trees in npm expose projects to removals and malicious updates.

thinEvidence.text: In TDD the unit of isolation is the test, not the class under test
thinEvidence.note: A definitional reading of Kent Beck's book rather than an empirical claim.

thinEvidence.text: Teams on a shared trunk can scale headcount up or down without losing throughput or quality
thinEvidence.note: Google's monorepo shows it is possible with heavy tooling investment; Brooks's-law effects do not vanish because of a branching model.

thinEvidence.text: Tech debt and distaste for old code alone are not a sufficient reason to rewrite a large successful product
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with Spolsky and with rewrite failure cases; opinion-based.

thinEvidence.text: A test suite with known gaps gives no decision value when it passes, so it cannot be trusted
thinEvidence.note: A framing about what trust in a suite means rather than a measurable outcome; partial suites still catch some regressions.

thinEvidence.text: Tests breaking during refactoring is a minor cost in practice
thinEvidence.note: Test co-evolution studies show test maintenance is a real and recurring effort, heavily dependent on how mock-heavy and implementation-coupled the tests are.

thinEvidence.text: Tests that are deterministic and independent of run order are more valuable because flaky results erode trust
thinEvidence.note: Flaky-test research at Google and in academia shows order dependence and nondeterminism waste developer time and cause ignored failures.

thinEvidence.text: Tests written to probe implementation details should be deleted once they have served their purpose
thinEvidence.note: A judgment about test maintenance trade-offs with no empirical comparison.

thinEvidence.text: There are no solutions in cloud architecture, only trade-offs
thinEvidence.note: Aphorism.

thinEvidence.text: Transformational leadership is necessary but not sufficient for high delivery performance.
thinEvidence.note: DORA found the bottom third of leaders half as likely to be high performers while top leaders were no better than median; one survey year.

thinEvidence.text: Trunk-based development only works with a fast comprehensive test suite and same-day code review
thinEvidence.note: Practitioner accounts and DORA both treat fast automated tests as a prerequisite for continuous delivery; synchronous review is one way to meet the merge cadence but not the only one.

thinEvidence.text: Trunk-based development requires developers to learn to work in small batches, which many find hard and resist
thinEvidence.note: Adoption reports consistently cite resistance; the magnitude is anecdotal.

thinEvidence.text: Type systems themselves contain soundness bugs that are hard to fix without breaking existing programs
thinEvidence.note: Eiffel covariance, Java generics with arrays, and unsoundness found in Scala and TypeScript are documented cases.

thinEvidence.text: Unit tests alone cannot catch integration errors, so a suite of only unit tests does not make code self-testing.
thinEvidence.note: By construction isolated unit tests do not exercise component interaction; integration failures are a well-documented defect class.

thinEvidence.text: Unit tests make it easy to set up edge-case contexts that are hard to reproduce in the full system
thinEvidence.note: Near-definitional and borne out by practice; error-handling paths in particular are hard to trigger end to end.

thinEvidence.text: Unit tests that never fail in version control still earn their keep because they fail transiently during development and are fixed before commit
thinEvidence.note: Local failures are invisible to repository history so 'never failed' undercounts value, but maintenance cost is real and tests that never fail even locally may be low value.

thinEvidence.text: Unmanaged technical debt undermines security because code and dependencies nobody understands cannot be reasoned about
thinEvidence.note: Dependency unawareness is a documented supply-chain risk; the link to general debt is argued rather than measured.

thinEvidence.text: Version control and code review let junior engineers write production code safely, replacing hierarchical chief-programmer teams
thinEvidence.note: Review and version control do gate bad code, but flatter teams also reflect cheaper compute; no causal study.

thinEvidence.text: Working as one group on one stream of work removes merge conflicts
thinEvidence.note: A single group working on one branch has nothing to merge, so this follows by construction and is consistently reported by mob teams.

thinEvidence.text: Working together builds psychological safety better than anything else
thinEvidence.note: Collaboration correlates with safety, but the superlative is attributed to unnamed research.

thinEvidence.text: Workspace design is a fundamental part of how a company takes care of its people
thinEvidence.note: A values statement.

thinEvidence.text: Writing down architecture decisions and their reasoning helps both humans and AI tools work on a codebase
thinEvidence.note: ADRs are widely adopted; the benefit is reported, not measured.
